# 📍 Locality Research Guide: Ohio — Pre-Statehood Period (circa 1785–1803)

---

## Jurisdictional Context & Boundary Changes

In 1790, there was no state of Ohio. The entire present-day state was part of the **Northwest Territory**, organized by the **Northwest Ordinance of 1787**. Ohio did not achieve statehood until **March 1, 1803**, making it the first state carved from the Northwest Territory.

**This is the single most important fact for research around 1790:** records created before 1803 are not filed under "Ohio" — they are filed under **Northwest Territory** or under the specific early county that held jurisdiction at the time. FamilySearch confirms this directly in its Ohio Genealogy wiki article (*"Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes"*).

### County Formation Timeline (the research trail)

| County | Organized | Area Covered | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Washington County** | 1788 | Southeastern Ohio (Marietta area) | First county; earliest territorial court at Marietta |
| **Hamilton County** | 1790 | Southwestern Ohio (Cincinnati area) | Second county; most active settlement zone in 1790 |
| *Remainder of Ohio* | —  | Unorganized territory | No county structure in 1790 |

If your ancestor was in Ohio around 1790, they were almost certainly in **Washington County** (if near the Ohio River east of the Scioto) or **Hamilton County** (if near Cincinnati). All other areas were unsettled or unorganized. **Search both county sets and the Northwest Territory record set together as one continuous research trail** — don't treat them as unrelated sources.

### Three Competing Land Systems

Ohio had three distinct survey and land-grant systems operating simultaneously, each with records in different repositories:

1. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami Rivers): Reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans. Used a metes-and-bounds survey — irregular lot shapes, described by landmarks. Warrants are held at the **Virginia State Library (Richmond, VA)**. These records predate Ohio statehood.

2. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): Surveyed on a separate township-range grid. Records are at the **Western Reserve Historical Society (WRHS), Cleveland**. Largely unsettled in 1790 but increasingly important by 1800.

3. **Federal Public Domain** (remainder of Ohio): Rectangular township survey system. Patents are at the **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO)** — searchable online at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov). This is a critical free, searchable database for early Ohio land.

> ⚠️ **Researcher must-know:** Determine which land district your ancestor's location falls in *before* searching land records — the three systems are held in different repositories with no overlap.

---

## Records Available for the 1785–1803 Period

### 1. Land Records ✅ Best Available Source

Land records are the **primary evidence source for pre-statehood Ohio** — they predate nearly all other record types and are the most systematic documentation of individuals in the territory.

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840* (Collection ID: 1542187) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images. Covers the overlap period from territorial organization through early statehood. **Indexed and searchable.**
- **FamilySearch Volume:** Image Group `005112233` — Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, **1788–1799**, 51 images. ⚠️ **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be examined image by image.
- **BLM GLO:** Federal land patents searchable online — an essential first stop for any pre-statehood land research in Ohio.
- **Virginia Military District warrants:** Virginia State Library, Richmond — for ancestors in the Scioto/Little Miami corridor.

### 2. Marriage Records ✅ Partially Available

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013* (Collection ID: 1803785) — 1,523,678 records, 761,839 images. The earliest records start in 1789, making this collection relevant for the period. **Indexed and searchable.**
- Marriages before 1803 were recorded by county courts (Washington and Hamilton counties). No statewide marriage registration existed.

### 3. Tax Records ✅ Available from 1800

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850* (Collection ID: 1987542) — 345,890 records. Covers the very end of the territorial period. **Indexed and searchable.**
- **FamilySearch Volume:** Image Group `005112240` — Washington County Tax Records, **1799–1803**, 73 images. ⚠️ **Mostly browse-only: only 12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.**
- Tax lists are extremely valuable as proxies for residence when no census or vital record exists.

### 4. Church Records ✅ Available

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950* (Collection ID: 2246917) — 678,234 records, 339,117 images. Starts in 1787, directly covering the territorial period. **Indexed and searchable.**
- Early denominations active in territorial Ohio include **Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Quaker** congregations — particularly in the Marietta (Washington County) and Cincinnati (Hamilton County) areas.
- Church registers often record baptisms, marriages, and burials that have no civil counterpart for this period.

### 5. Federal Census ⚠️ Limited / No Coverage for Ohio in 1790

- The **1790 federal census** was conducted, but Ohio (as Northwest Territory) was not fully enumerated. Settlement was sparse and dangerous; no complete territorial census was taken for the Ohio region in 1790.
- The **1800 federal census** is the first to meaningfully cover Ohio, at which point Washington and Hamilton counties are enumerated. This is the earliest reliable census starting point.
- No state or territorial census was conducted for Ohio before statehood.

### 6. Death Records ❌ Not Available for This Period

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001* (Collection ID: 1417891) — starts in 1840, well after the target period.
- No civil death registration existed in territorial or early statehood Ohio. Church burial registers (see above) are the only systematic death documentation.

### 7. Military Records ✅ Critical Substitute Source

- Revolutionary War service and pension records at **NARA** (searchable via Fold3 and Ancestry) are essential — many early Ohio settlers were veterans who received bounty land in the Virginia Military District.
- The **Fold3** platform (curated external link returned for Ohio) holds military service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants covering the 1780s–1800s.
- The **National Archives** (NARA) holds Northwest Territory administrative and military records.

### 8. Probate & Court Records ✅ Partially Available

- Territorial court records for Washington County (Marietta) are held at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus — the wiki confirms this is the primary state-level repository for early territorial and court records.
- Hamilton County probate and court records begin 1790 at the county level.
- These records can document family relationships, guardianships, and estate inventories when vital records don't exist.

---

## Where Records Are Held

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Ohio History Connection, Columbus** | Territorial records, early court records, state archives — primary starting point |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents, pre-statehood and early statehood |
| **Virginia State Library, Richmond VA** | Virginia Military District warrants and surveys |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland** | Connecticut Western Reserve land records |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Northwest Territory admin records, military service, pensions, bounty land |
| **Washington County Courthouse, Marietta OH** | Earliest county deed, probate, and court records (1788+) |
| **Hamilton County Courthouse, Cincinnati OH** | Second county records (1790+) |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Digitized collections above (land, marriages, church, tax) |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service, pension, and bounty land files |

---

## Key Researcher Warnings

1. **Search "Northwest Territory" AND early Ohio county names together.** Records from 1788–1803 may be filed under either jurisdiction. Treat them as one continuous research trail.
2. **The 1790 census did not cover Ohio.** Do not expect to find your ancestor there. Begin census research with 1800.
3. **Determine land district first.** Virginia Military District, Connecticut Western Reserve, and federal public domain records are in completely different repositories with no overlap.
4. **Two volumes are browse-only.** The Northwest Territory Land Records (005112233, 0% indexed) and Washington County Tax Records (005112240, 12% indexed) must be browsed image by image — plan extra time.
5. **Church records start in 1787** and are your best substitute for missing vital events in this period — search the FamilySearch *Ohio, Church Records* collection first for baptisms and burials.
6. **No statewide death registration** existed until decades after statehood. Burial evidence comes entirely from church registers or cemetery transcriptions.

---

## Summary: Research Strategy for Ohio circa 1790

Given the documentation gaps, approach this period in this order:

1. **Land records first** — BLM GLO patents + FamilySearch *Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840* to place the person geographically
2. **Determine county** — Washington (1788) or Hamilton (1790)? Or unorganized territory?
3. **Tax lists** — FamilySearch *Ohio, Tax Records* and the browse-only Washington County volume for presence evidence
4. **Church records** — *Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950* for vital events that have no civil equivalent
5. **Marriage records** — *Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013* for the earliest county-level marriage bonds
6. **Military/pension records** — NARA/Fold3 for Revolutionary War veterans who settled in the Virginia Military District
7. **Probate and court records** — Ohio History Connection for territorial court records; county courthouses for local records
8. **1800 census** — first reliable census enumeration for Ohio residents

The documentation gaps around 1790 are real but bridgeable — land, tax, church, and military records together provide a strong substitute framework when civil vital registration simply did not exist.

# 📍 Locality Research Guide: California, 1848–1865
### Gold Rush–Era Miners and Settlers

---

## Jurisdictional Context

California became the 31st U.S. state on **September 9, 1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely — meaning there are **no territorial-era government records** for the pre-statehood Gold Rush years (1848–1850). The rush began January 24, 1848, when gold was found at Sutter's Mill in Coloma. An estimated **300,000 people** poured into California, arriving by sea (around Cape Horn or via the Panama crossing) and overland. County governments formed rapidly but unevenly; civil infrastructure was sparse, especially in the mining counties of the Sierra Nevada foothills, during 1848–1852.

**Critical gaps to know upfront:**
- California did not require **statewide civil registration** of births or deaths until **1905**. For the 1850s, civil vital records exist only at the county level and survival is incomplete.
- The **1850 federal census** (California's first) was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing entirely.
- The **Great Registers** (voter registration) are a major Gold Rush–era substitute source but do not begin until **1866**, just after the core Rush period.

---

## Record Types, Availability & Access

### 1. 📋 Census Records
| Record | Years | FamilySearch Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| California State Census | 1852 | **Indexed + full-text searchable** (88% name-indexed; imageGroupNumber 006601001, 522 images) | The single most important snapshot of the Gold Rush population at its peak |
| U.S. Federal Census | 1850, 1860 | Indexed on FamilySearch & Ancestry | 1850 returns for several mining counties are **missing/destroyed**; 1860 is intact |

**Strategy:** Start with the 1852 state census — it captures the Rush population at its peak, before many miners left. Then use 1860 federal census to track who stayed. The FamilySearch California State Census volume (imageGroupNumber 006601001) is both name-indexed and full-text searchable.

---

### 2. ⛏️ Mining Claim Registers
| Record | Years | FamilySearch Access | Repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mining Claim Registers (San Francisco) | 1849–1855 | **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable (340 images, imageGroupNumber 006601002) | County Recorders' offices; originals at county courthouses |

Mining claims were filed at **county recorders' offices**, not centrally. These registers list the claimant's name, description of the claim, location, and often witnesses. They are among the most direct Gold Rush records but must be browsed image-by-image on FamilySearch. **The mother lode counties** (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, etc.) each have their own records — identify which county your ancestor mined before searching. FamilySearch's wiki notes these are held at county recorders' offices; originals may also be at the California State Archives in Sacramento.

---

### 3. 🚢 Arrival Records (Ship Passenger Manifests)
| Record | Years | FamilySearch Access | Repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| Port Arrival Registers (Sacramento) | 1849–1858 | **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable (298 images, imageGroupNumber 006601003) | NARA, San Bruno, CA |
| San Francisco ship passenger lists | 1848–1860s | Indexed at Ancestry; partial on FamilySearch | NARA San Bruno; microfilm at FamilySearch |

Per the FamilySearch Wiki "California Genealogy" article, **ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals** are held at the **National Archives, San Bruno, California** (NARA Pacific Region). Most "49ers" arrived by ship — either around Cape Horn or via the Panama isthmus route. These manifests often record the port of embarkation, name, age, occupation, and sometimes origin. Ancestry.com has the indexed U.S. Federal Census collection and supplementary passenger record sets; NARA is the authoritative repository for original manifests.

**Note on overland arrivals:** Those who came via the California, Oregon, or Santa Fe Trails left far fewer institutional records. Overland trail journals, diaries, and emigrant guide lists at the **Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** and **California State Library** are the best substitute sources.

---

### 4. 👥 Voter Registration — Great Registers
| Collection | Years | FamilySearch Access |
|---|---|---|
| California, Great Registers, 1866–1910 | 1866–1910 | **Indexed** — 1,345,678 records (collection 1923340) |

The Great Registers begin just after the core Gold Rush era, but they are invaluable for identifying men who **arrived during the Rush and stayed**. They record name, age, occupation, physical description, birthplace, and nativity — often with naturalization details for foreign-born miners. Search these even if your ancestor arrived in the 1850s; the first register (1866) captures the settled survivor population.

---

### 5. 🏛️ Vital Records — Births & Marriages
| Collection | Years | FamilySearch Access |
|---|---|---|
| California, County Births, 1850–1919 | 1850–1919 | **Indexed** — 789,456 records (collection 2017276) |
| California, County Marriages, 1850–1952 | 1850–1952 | **Indexed** — 567,890 persons (collection 1452832) |

⚠️ **Important caveat:** These are *county-level* records, not statewide registrations. For the 1850s, registration was inconsistent and survival is uneven — many counties simply did not maintain reliable registers in their earliest years. Treat an absence of a birth or death record as a coverage gap, not evidence the event did not occur. Church records (see below) often fill the void.

---

### 6. ⛪ Church Records
No dedicated California church record volume appeared in the FamilySearch volume search for 1848–1865. However:
- **Catholic parish registers** for Gold Rush–era California exist at diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco; Diocese of Sacramento).
- **Protestant denominations** — Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist — established congregations quickly in the mining towns; records are held at denominational archives or local historical societies.
- **Mission Records, 1769–1850** (FamilySearch collection 1804372, 98,765 records): These are pre-statehood Spanish/Mexican-era records (baptisms, marriages, burials by Franciscan friars). Relevant only for families with deep California roots predating the Rush.

---

### 7. 🗺️ Land Records
- **Federal land patents** for California are searchable via the **BLM General Land Office (GLO) website** (glorecords.blm.gov). California is a federal land state; original patents from 1850 onward are online.
- **County deed books** at county courthouses and the California State Archives document land purchases and transfers — miners who transitioned to farming or town lots often appear here.
- **Mexican land grant records** (pre-statehood ranchos) are relevant for families already in California before 1848; held at the California State Archives and the Bancroft Library.

---

### 8. ⚖️ Court & Naturalization Records
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — county, state, or federal. For California's Gold Rush foreign-born population (Chilean, Mexican, Chinese, German, Irish, Australian miners), check county superior court records and federal district court records at **NARA San Bruno**.
- Foreign miners were subject to the **Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, 1852)** — tax collector rolls, where they survive, name foreign-born miners and their nationality. These are at county archives.
- **County court records** (probate, guardianship, civil suits) are at county courthouses and the California State Archives.

---

### 9. 💀 Cemetery & Death Records
- **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) has transcribed many California Gold Rush–era burial sites, including Gold Hill, Coloma, and Placerville cemeteries.
- Death records for the 1850s are extremely sparse at the county level (civil registration was voluntary and uneven). **Mortality Schedules** of the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses record persons who died in the year preceding the census — these are a key substitute source.
- **Newspaper obituaries** in Gold Rush–era California newspapers are another substitute; many are digitized at **Newspapers.com** and the **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (cdnc.ucr.edu — free).

---

### 10. 📰 Newspapers
- Gold Rush California had a vigorous press; newspapers documented arrivals, deaths, mining claims, and legal notices.
- **Newspapers.com** (subscription) and the **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (free, cdnc.ucr.edu) are the primary access points.
- The *Alta California* (San Francisco, 1849 onward) is one of the most important Gold Rush–era papers.

---

### 11. 🎖️ Military Records
- **Fold3** and NARA hold service records and pension files for men who served in the Mexican-American War (which ended just before the Rush) or the Civil War, both of which bracket the 1850s.
- California had no major Civil War battles, but many Gold Rush–era men enlisted in the Union Army; pension files often contain detailed biographical data including pre-California origins.

---

### 12. 📚 Manuscript & Special Collections
Per the FamilySearch Wiki "California Genealogy" article, two repositories hold extensive Gold Rush–era manuscript collections not available online:
- **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** — overland diaries, journals, letters, and Gold Rush memoir collections
- **California State Library, Sacramento** — manuscript collections, Gold Rush–era newspapers, and county histories

These are physical repositories requiring on-site or request access.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | State census 1852 (indexed), county births/marriages, Great Registers, Mission records, some mining/arrival volumes | Free online |
| NARA San Bruno (Pacific Region) | San Francisco passenger manifests, naturalization records, federal court records | On-site or digitized portions at Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | County court records, land records, Great Registers originals | On-site; some digitized |
| Ancestry.com | 1850/1860 federal census (indexed), passenger lists, newspapers | Subscription |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Overland diaries, Gold Rush manuscripts | On-site request |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Newspapers, county histories, manuscripts | On-site; some digitized |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from 1850 | Free online |
| County Recorders' offices | Mining claim registers, deed books | On-site; some on FamilySearch |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions | Free online |
| Newspapers.com / CDNC | Historical newspapers | Subscription / Free |

---

## Research Quirks & Warnings

1. **California skipped territorial status** — there are no territorial government records. The pre-statehood period (1848–Sep 1850) produced very few institutional records of any kind.
2. **The 1850 federal census is partially destroyed** — some Gold Rush county returns (including parts of El Dorado) are missing. The 1852 state census is the critical substitute.
3. **Great Registers begin in 1866**, after the core Rush. Search them for men who stayed and settled — they are the best-indexed large name database for Gold Rush survivors.
4. **Mining claims are county-level, browse-only on FamilySearch** — identify the specific mining county before searching; do not expect a statewide index.
5. **Civil registration of births/deaths was not statewide until 1905** — 1850s county records are incomplete and uneven. Use mortality schedules, church records, and newspapers as substitutes.
6. **FamilySearch has 14 digitized volumes** for California 1848–1865 (first page returned 3 — the state census, mining claim registers, and port arrival registers); browse the full volume list at FamilySearch for additional record sets not surfaced here.
7. **Foreign Miners' Tax rolls** (1850, 1852) name foreign-born miners by nationality — check county archives for these if your ancestor was not American-born.

---

# Locality Guide: New York City — Colonial Period (1700–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Founded as New Amsterdam by the Dutch West India Company in 1624/1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York. The 1700s fall entirely within the British colonial period (1664–1783).
- **Administrative center:** Manhattan Island (the core of colonial NYC); the city was divided into wards, each with its own tax and administrative records.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British Crown colony). After the Revolution, jurisdiction passed to the State of New York (1783).
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tools for this fixture. Historical sources outside this survey estimate roughly 5,000–25,000 inhabitants across the century, making this one of the largest colonial cities in North America.
- **Economy:** A major Atlantic port — shipping, trade, mercantile commerce, and skilled artisan trades dominate. Port records and merchant activity generate ancillary records.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Dutch-descended families alongside growing English, Huguenot (French Protestant), and Jewish communities; a large enslaved African population.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous congregation), Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church, founded 1697), Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot), Jewish (Shearith Israel, oldest synagogue in North America, founded 1654). Each denomination kept its own registers.
- **Key historical events:** British military occupation of NYC during the Revolution (1776–1783) disrupted civic life and record-keeping; a major fire in 1776 destroyed portions of lower Manhattan.

---

## Boundary changes

- The 1700s target period falls entirely within the colonial Province of New York; no boundary reorganization split the city's records across competing jurisdictions during this period.
- Records generated before 1664 (Dutch period) are at the city and provincial level; some are in Dutch and held at the New York State Archives and the New-York Historical Society.
- After 1783 the jurisdiction transitioned from provincial (Prerogative Court of New York, Mayor's Court) to state and municipal administration — records created post-Revolution are held under different institutional custody.
- Modern New York City (five boroughs consolidated in 1898) is far larger than colonial NYC, which centered on Manhattan. Do not expect borough-level organization in colonial records.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** New York State did not require civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1880. **No civil vital records exist for the 1700s.**
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the only systematic vital record source for this period. See Church Records below.

---

### Church records
*The single most important source class for colonial NYC genealogy.*

- **Denominations present (from FamilySearch Wiki, "New York City Genealogy"):** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous series, registers begin 1639), Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, and others (Lutheran, Huguenot, Jewish kehilla records at Shearith Israel).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; some confirmations and membership rolls.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **New York, Church Records, 1640–1940** (Collection ID 1469062) — date range overlaps the colonial period. This is one of five indexed collections returned for New York state.
- **Digitized volume:** FamilySearch holds one digitized image volume of **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700–1776** for New York City (Image Group 007733180 — 211 images):
  - `recordSearchablePercent`: **0%** — not name-indexed
  - `fulltextSearchable`: **false**
  - **Language: Dutch** — must be read in the original language
  - **Access level: Browse-only images** — must be examined page by page with no search capability; researcher must be able to read 18th-century Dutch handwriting
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (browse-only for the Dutch Reformed volume above); the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society hold extensive colonial-era church collections (per FamilySearch Wiki). Individual parish archives (Trinity Church archives, for example) hold original registers.
- **⚠️ Language note:** Dutch Reformed records through the mid-1700s may be partially or entirely in Dutch.

---

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was 1790 — just outside the colonial target period, but useful for families present at the end of this era.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No formal colonial census equivalent to a modern census existed for the 1700s. **Tax lists and militia rolls (see below) serve as the primary population-listing substitutes.**
- No colonial NYC census volumes were returned by `volume_search` for the 1700–1783 window.

---

### Probate records
- **Court of jurisdiction:** The **Prerogative Court of New York** had colony-wide probate jurisdiction during the colonial period. Wills proved there are indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the **New-York Historical Society** (per FamilySearch Wiki, "New York City Genealogy").
- **FamilySearch collection:** **New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971** (Collection ID 1542780) — date range covers the colonial period.
- **Research value:** Wills and estate inventories name heirs, creditors, and executors — a critical source when church records are unavailable or ambiguous.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collection 1542780); New York State Archives; New-York Historical Society (Abstracts of Wills finding aid).

---

### Land records
- **System:** Metes and bounds (not the later rectangular survey system). Colonial land grants were issued by the royal governor; city lot conveyances were recorded at the municipal level.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **New York, Land Records, 1630–1975** (Collection ID 2078654) — date range covers the colonial period.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, and land conveyances (per FamilySearch Wiki, "New York City Genealogy").
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collection 2078654); New York State Archives (colonial patents and grants); New York City municipal archives (deed books).

---

### Court records
- **Mayor's Court:** The primary civil and criminal court for colonial NYC. Records from the Mayor's Court are identified in FamilySearch Wiki ("New York City Genealogy") as a key source for the 1700s.
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Held at the **New York State Archives**; cover provincial governance and contain references to residents (per FamilySearch Wiki).
- **Access level:** These are **physical/archival** records — not available through major online databases. Researchers must contact the New York State Archives or the New-York Historical Society directly.

---

### Military records
- **Colonial militia rolls:** The Province of New York maintained militia rolls listing men of military age, useful for identifying adult male residents (per FamilySearch Wiki, "New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records").
- **Revolutionary War:** For families at the end of the target period (c. 1775–1783), Loyalist records and British Army records are relevant; Patriot service records are at NARA (Fold3, per external links returned).
- **Where held:** Fold3 (military records — returned in external links); NARA; New York State Archives (colonial militia).

---

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards of colonial NYC (per FamilySearch Wiki, "New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records"). These are ward-by-ward property assessments.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804** (Collection ID 1678432) — dates 1799–1804, which fall *after* the colonial period (post-1783). This collection is not a colonial source but covers the immediate post-Revolutionary generation of the same families.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial-era tax lists are the closest substitute for a census in the 1700s — they list heads of household by ward, enabling rough enumeration of the population.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; New-York Historical Society; some city records at NYC Municipal Archives.

---

### Cemetery records
- **Major colonial cemeteries:** Trinity Church (Anglican) burial ground on lower Broadway; Dutch Reformed church burial grounds; Jewish cemetery at Shearith Israel (oldest Jewish cemetery in North America, burials from 1683).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (returned in external links) covers some colonial-era burials, but coverage for 1700s stones is incomplete.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for Trinity Church and other major parishes are held in their respective archives. Many burial grounds were disrupted during the British occupation (1776–1783).

---

### Newspaper records
- **Colonial papers:** The *New-York Gazette* (founded 1725) and *New-York Weekly Journal* (founded 1733) are the principal 1700s newspapers for NYC. They contain legal notices, ship arrivals, runaway servant/slave notices, and some death notices.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (returned in external links — subscription); some titles available through the Library of Congress *Chronicling America* project (free).
- **Content value:** Legal notices (estate settlements, property disputes), ship manifests, and community announcements supplement official records.

---

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Port of New York:** One of the busiest colonial-era ports. Passenger arrival lists for the 1700s are fragmentary compared to 19th-century records — no systematic manifests were required until 1820.
- **Surviving colonial arrivals:** Some ship lists exist in colonial newspapers and provincial records; the New-York Historical Society and NARA hold partial series.
- **NARA:** Returned in external links; holds the earliest federal-era passenger lists (post-1820) and some colonial-era naturalization records.
- **Naturalization:** Prior to 1906, naturalizations could occur in any court of record. The Mayor's Court and the Court of Chancery of New York Province granted naturalizations; these are embedded in court record series.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | New York, Church Records, 1640–1940 (ID 1469062); New York, Land Records, 1630–1975 (ID 2078654); New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971 (ID 1542780); Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700–1776 (browse-only, Dutch) | Free |
| **Fold3** | Military records including colonial and Revolutionary War materials | Subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1790+); some church and vital record databases | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records (partial coverage) | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspaper archive including colonial titles | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Federal records, naturalization, military pension files | Free access; some via Fold3/Ancestry |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| **New York State Archives** (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts; provincial court records; colonial land grants and patents | In-person or written inquiry; some finding aids online |
| **New-York Historical Society** (NYC) | Extensive colonial-era collections; *Abstracts of Wills* series; church and community records | In-person; some digitized; library membership |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** (NYC) | Colonial NYC genealogy collections; published abstracts and indexes | Membership; some databases online |
| **NYC Municipal Archives** | City ward records; some colonial-era deed books | In-person; online portal for select records |
| **Trinity Church Archives** (NYC) | Anglican baptism, marriage, and burial registers from 1697 | Appointment; some published in print |
| **Congregation Shearith Israel Archives** (NYC) | Colonial-era Jewish community records (burial, membership) | Contact congregation |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types are confirmed as existing but are **not** available through major online databases and require physical or archival access:

- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** (New York State Archives) — provincial governance records naming colonial residents
- **Mayor's Court records** (New York City) — civil and criminal proceedings, naturalizations
- **Colonial-era militia rolls** — ward and provincial level
- **Colonial-era tax assessment lists** for most ward-years (the FamilySearch tax collection starts 1799, after the colonial period)
- **Most individual church registers** beyond the one Dutch Reformed volume on FamilySearch — Trinity Church, Presbyterian, Lutheran, and Huguenot registers are largely in institutional archives
- **Jewish community records** (Shearith Israel) — must contact the congregation

---

## Known record losses

- **Great Fire of 1776:** A large fire during the British military takeover of New York City in September 1776 destroyed roughly one-quarter of the city. Some church and civic records were lost or displaced.
- **British occupation (1776–1783):** Seven years of military occupation disrupted civic record-keeping. Court records and municipal registers from this period may be incomplete or irregular.
- **General colonial-era attrition:** Paper records from the 1700s that were never microfilmed or institutionally preserved are susceptible to loss. Not all ward tax lists or Mayor's Court volumes survive intact.

---

## Research tips

1. **Church records are your vital records.** New York had no civil registration until 1880. For any birth, marriage, or death event in the 1700s, start with the church the family attended — Dutch Reformed, Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, or another denomination.

2. **The Dutch Reformed Church Registers (1700–1776) on FamilySearch are browse-only and in Dutch.** Image Group 007733180 has 211 images but 0% name-indexing and no full-text search. You must scroll image by image and read 18th-century Dutch script. Consider using a translation resource or professional assistant.

3. **The *Abstracts of Wills* series is your probate index.** Wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York are abstracted and indexed in volumes published by the New-York Historical Society — consult these before ordering original probate files.

4. **Tax lists stand in for the census.** The first federal census (1790) postdates the colonial period. Ward-level tax assessment lists are the best substitute for identifying a household's presence in a given year and neighborhood.

5. **Militia rolls identify adult men.** Colonial New York Province militia rolls list men of military age and can confirm a man's presence in the colony at a given date.

6. **Search by ward, not just by name.** Colonial NYC was organized into wards (e.g., South Ward, Dock Ward, East Ward). Knowing which ward a family lived in narrows the search within unindexed volumes.

7. **The NYGBS and New-York Historical Society publish finding aids.** Before ordering records from archives, check whether the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society or the NYHS has published an abstract, index, or calendar for the record series you need — these save significant research time.

8. **For Revolutionary-era families (c. 1775–1783), check both Patriot and Loyalist records.** NYC was a Loyalist stronghold during the occupation. Some families appear in British Army rolls, Loyalist claims (held at The National Archives, Kew, UK), or refugee records.

9. **Colonial newspapers supplement official records.** The *New-York Gazette* (1725+) and *New-York Weekly Journal* (1733+) published ship arrivals, estate notices, runaway notices, and community announcements that can place individuals in a time and place.

10. **The FamilySearch wiki page "[New York City Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy)" is the starting reference.** It covers colonial sources in depth and should be consulted for collection-specific guidance beyond what this survey covers.

The FamilySearch wiki place pages for New York returned generic content rather than New York-specific guidance; the FamilySearch Wiki "New York City Genealogy" article (retrieved via wiki_search) provided the key colonial-record specifics cited above.*

# Locality Guide: Virginia (American Revolutionary War, 1775–1783)
**Focus: Military Service and Wartime Activities**

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Status during period:** Virginia was a royal colony transitioning to an independent commonwealth. Its colonial assembly declared independence in 1776; formal U.S. Constitutional ratification came in 1788.
- **Administrative structure:** County-level governance established as early as the 1630s — one of the most mature county record systems in British North America. Counties held authority over land, probate, courts, and militia organization.
- **Territory in 1775–1783:** Much larger than modern Virginia. What are now **Kentucky** (separate state 1792) and **West Virginia** (separate state 1863) were Virginia counties during the war. Ancestors located in those modern states during this period appear in **Virginia** records.
- **Population:** No tool data returned for this period. Virginia was the most populous of the original thirteen colonies; estimates place its population at roughly 500,000–600,000 in the 1770s, including a large enslaved population.
- **Economy:** Tobacco agriculture (tidewater/piedmont), subsistence farming (backcountry), maritime trade.
- **Military role:** Per the FamilySearch wiki article *Virginia Military Records*, Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony. The decisive battle of Yorktown (1781) was fought on Virginia soil.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Stable internally** during 1775–1783, but Virginia's western frontier was actively expanding via county formation.
- **Kentucky counties formed from Virginia:** Fayette, Jefferson, and Lincoln counties organized 1780; all three were Virginia counties until Kentucky statehood (1792).
- **West Virginia** did not separate until 1863 — all trans-Allegheny Virginia records from the war period are Virginia records.
- **Practical rule:** If your ancestor lived in modern Kentucky or West Virginia during the Revolution, start your search in Virginia county records, not Kentucky or West Virginia repositories.

---

## Available Record Types

### 🎯 Military Records — Primary Focus

This is the richest category for your research question. Per the FamilySearch wiki article *[Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*:

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Continental Line service records & muster rolls** | NARA, Record Group 93 | Fold3 (subscription); some free on FamilySearch |
| **Pension & bounty-land warrant applications** | NARA, Record Group 15 | Fold3; Ancestry; some on FamilySearch |
| **Virginia militia records** | Library of Virginia, Richmond | Partially digitized; some on FamilySearch |
| **Virginia State Navy records** (published) | Library of Virginia; printed volumes | Physical / interlibrary loan |
| **Bounty land warrants — Virginia Military District (Ohio)** | Virginia State Library / NARA | Physical and some digitized |

**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783* (collection ID 1945678) — 345,678 records, 172,839 images — directly covering your target period. Available at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678).

**Fold3** (subscription, via external links search) is the leading online repository for NARA military records including Revolutionary War pension files and compiled service records.

> ⚠️ **Important distinction:** Many Virginia men served in *both* the Continental Army and the state militia at different times. Check both record sets — Continental service is documented at NARA; militia service is primarily at the Library of Virginia.

**Pension files** are among the most genealogically rich records of the era. Successful pension applications often include the veteran's sworn narrative of service, names of officers, and sometimes family information. Widow's pension applications (filed after 1836) commonly include marriage details.

**Bounty land:** Virginia issued warrants for land in the *Virginia Military District of Ohio* to its veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to specific land claims and can confirm service.

---

### Tax Records — Critical Census Substitute

Virginia's 1790 federal census was **destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. The primary substitute is county personal property tax lists, which begin in **1782–1783**.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850* (collection ID 1456723) — 456,789 records, 228,394 images — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723).

- Lists taxable males (typically 16+) by name within each county
- Useful for locating a family's county of residence in the immediate post-war period
- Sequential years can track a family's movement between counties
- Tithables lists from the colonial period (pre-1782) provide earlier coverage

---

### Land Records

Virginia is a **state-land state** (metes-and-bounds survey system, not rectangular). Land grants were issued by the colonial governor / Commonwealth, not the federal government.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900* (collection ID 1734285) — 2,567,890 records, 1,283,945 images — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285).

Key sub-types:
- **Northern Neck Proprietary grants** (Lord Fairfax's territory — northern Virginia)
- **Colonial land patents** (Secretary of State's office)
- **Deed books** (county courthouse level)
- **Bounty land warrants / surveys** for veterans (see Military above)

The Library of Virginia holds Virginia Land Office records. The Bureau of Land Management GLO website applies only to *federal-land states* — Virginia is not one.

---

### Church Records

There was **no civil vital registration** in Virginia until 1853. Church records are the primary vital records source for this period.

The **Church of England (Anglican)** was Virginia's established church until 1776 disestablishment. Parish registers (vestry books) recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials. After disestablishment, the Episcopal Church continued many of these congregations; other denominations (Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist) grew rapidly in the 1780s.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929* (collection ID 1598230) — 1,234,567 records, 617,283 images — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230).

- **Anglican/Episcopal vestry books** are the richest wartime vital source; many are digitized or on microfilm
- Baptist and Presbyterian congregations formed in the backcountry during and after the war — their earliest registers may document soldiers' families
- The **Library of Virginia** and **Virginia Historical Society** hold many original vestry books

---

### Vital Records (Civil)

- **Civil registration began: 1853** — entirely outside this period.
- For 1775–1783: rely on church registers, county court marriage bonds and licenses (county level), and probate/estate records for death evidence.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900* (collection ID 1734285) also covers marriage bonds and licenses from this era.

---

### Probate & Court Records

Wartime deaths generated estate records — wills, inventories, guardianship appointments for minor children. These are held at the **county courthouse** level and are often well-preserved.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920* (collection ID 2134567) — 1,789,012 records, 894,506 images — [familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567).

This collection spans county order books, minute books, deed books, and related court records. Particularly useful for:
- Guardianship of soldiers' orphans
- Administration of intestate estates of men killed in service
- County court minute books documenting local wartime governance

---

### Census Records

- **No federal census** during 1775–1783 (first federal census: 1790).
- The **1790 Virginia census was destroyed** (see Tax Records above for the critical substitute).
- The **1800 census** is the earliest surviving federal enumeration for Virginia.
- Colonial-era **quitrent rolls** and **tithable lists** predate the war and can place families before 1775.

---

### Newspaper Records

- The **Virginia Gazette** (Williamsburg) was the primary colonial newspaper, published throughout most of the war. It carried militia notices, casualty reports, legal notices, and estate advertisements.
- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription) holds some Virginia colonial newspaper content.
- The **Library of Virginia** and **College of William & Mary** hold microfilm of the Virginia Gazette.

---

### Cemetery Records

- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) (free) — online cemetery indexing; coverage varies by county and church
- Many Revolutionary-era graves are in churchyard cemeteries (Anglican/Episcopal), private family plots, or small community cemeteries; physical access or local historical society contact may be required
- Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) and local genealogical societies have documented many veterans' graves

---

---

## Records NOT Online

- **Original NARA pension and service record files** — digital images on Fold3/Ancestry are reproductions; the originals remain at NARA and can be ordered directly
- **Virginia State Navy records** — published in printed volumes; physical or interlibrary loan
- **Many vestry books** still held by individual Episcopal parishes or county courthouses — not yet digitized
- **Some county deed and order books** exist only as physical volumes at county courthouses
- **Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty land surveys** — partially available; some require direct Library of Virginia inquiry

---

## Known Record Losses

| Loss | Cause | Substitute |
|---|---|---|
| **1790 Virginia federal census** | British burned Washington, 1814 | County personal property tax lists, 1782–1785 |
| **Many county courthouse records** | Courthouse fires (numerous throughout 19th–20th c.) | State-level copies; published abstracts; DAR transcriptions |
| **Anglican vestry books** (some) | Church disestablishment chaos post-1776 | Baptist/Presbyterian registers for same communities; county court marriage bonds |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with pension files.** Revolutionary War pension applications at NARA (RG 15) are among the most genealogically detailed records of the era. A veteran's sworn statement of service often names officers, battle locations, and comrades. Widow applications can document marriages. Search Fold3 or Ancestry for digitized images.

2. **Check both Continental Army and militia records separately.** Virginia men rotated between both. NARA holds Continental records; the Library of Virginia is the primary repository for militia documentation (per *Virginia Military Records* wiki).

3. **Use 1782–1785 tax lists in place of the 1790 census.** The 1790 Virginia census no longer exists. The earliest surviving federal enumeration is 1800. Personal property tax lists beginning 1782 are the best available substitute and are available through FamilySearch's *Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850* collection.

4. **Virginia is a state-land state.** Do not search the BLM General Land Office (GLO) website for Virginia land patents — that site covers federal-land states only. Virginia grants were issued by the colonial/Commonwealth government; search the Library of Virginia's land office records and the FamilySearch *Land, Marriage, and Will Records* collection.

5. **If the ancestor was in modern Kentucky or West Virginia:** Search Virginia county records for the relevant 1775–1783 county. Kentucky and West Virginia did not exist as separate states during the Revolutionary War.

6. **Look for bounty land warrants in Ohio.** Virginia's Military District of Ohio (now south-central Ohio) was the bounty land grant area for Virginia veterans. If a veteran later appears in Ohio, warrant records connect Ohio land to Virginia service.

7. **DAR lineage papers.** The Daughters of the American Revolution has documented hundreds of thousands of Virginia Revolutionary War patriot lineages. Their database can corroborate service and link veterans to descendants whose applications cite primary sources.

8. **Search the Virginia Gazette.** Williamsburg's colonial newspaper carried militia musters, runaway servant/slave notices, estate advertisements, and wartime community news throughout the 1775–1783 period.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (Early 1800s, c. 1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **City / Parish:** New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (parish seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** State of Louisiana (from 1812); Orleans Territory (1804–1812); part of the Louisiana Purchase territory from the United States (1803); briefly under French rule (1800–1803); Spanish colonial rule before that
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this fixture; historically the city grew from roughly 8,000 in 1800 to over 100,000 by 1840, making it one of the largest U.S. cities
- **Economy:** Port trade, cotton, sugar, enslaved labor, banking, commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American (post-1803), free persons of color (*gens de couleur libres*), enslaved Africans, Haitian refugees (especially post-1809), German and Irish immigrants
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral, the oldest cathedral in the U.S.); also Protestant congregations after American takeover
- **Legal system:** **Civil law** (not common law) — Louisiana's unique French/Spanish legal heritage means records use distinctive terminology: *successions* (not probate), *tutorships* (not guardianship), *interdictions*, and extensive notarial documentation of private legal acts
- **Key historical events:** Great Fire of 1788, Second Great Fire of 1794, Louisiana Purchase 1803, Battle of New Orleans 1815, yellow fever epidemics (1817, 1819, 1820s–1850s), massive immigration waves

---

## Boundary and Jurisdictional History

The early 1800s span **four governing regimes** — a critically important fact for record-seeking:

| Period | Governing Authority | Record Language | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before 1800 | Spanish colonial (Cabildo) | Spanish, French | Notarial and church records |
| 1800–1803 | French (briefly) | French | Minimal distinct records |
| 1803–1804 | U.S. (District of Orleans) | English, French | Louisiana Purchase transition |
| 1804–1812 | Orleans Territory (U.S.) | English, French | Territorial government records |
| 1812– | State of Louisiana | English, French | Statehood; parish system retained |

**Orleans Parish** was established as Louisiana's parish equivalent of a county at statehood in 1812. Records created before 1812 under territorial or colonial authority are filed under the predecessor jurisdictions. The **Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge** holds territorial and early state records per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records").

---

## Known Record Losses — Disasters and Survival

> Per the FamilySearch Wiki article "New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters":

### Fires of 1788 and 1794
- **Great Fire of March 21, 1788** — destroyed approximately 856 buildings in the French Quarter, including many colonial administrative records
- **Second Great Fire of December 8, 1794** — destroyed approximately 212 additional structures
- Together, these fires destroyed **most of the original French colonial-era buildings and many civic records** of the Spanish colonial administration

### What Survived Despite the Fires

Four categories of records survived because they were held separately from the burned structures or because copies existed:

1. **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — Baptisms, marriages, and burials from **1731** survive, though with gaps caused by the fires. These are the single most important genealogical source for New Orleans families in this period. Held at the Archdiocese of New Orleans and Louisiana State University.

2. **Notarial Acts** — The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds **over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734**. Under the civil law system, virtually every significant private legal transaction — property sales, contracts, wills, manumissions of enslaved persons, business agreements — was recorded before a notary. Spanish colonial practice often required duplicate copies, which improved survival.

3. **Cabildo records** — Records of the Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body) survive and are held at the Louisiana State Museum and Louisiana State Archives.

4. **Post-1803 U.S. records** — Federal and territorial records created after the Louisiana Purchase survived intact, as they postdate the fires.

### Flooding
New Orleans's chronic flooding created ongoing paper deterioration risks for records stored in basements or low-lying buildings throughout the 19th century. This is a diffuse rather than acute loss, but researchers should expect gaps in parish-level registers and courthouse records.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** Louisiana did **not** have statewide civil registration until **1914**. Before that date, civil registration existed only intermittently and locally.
- **Early 1800s:** No systematic civil vital records exist for this period. The primary substitute is **church sacramental registers** (see below).
- **Death index from 1819:** FamilySearch has a **Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964** (collection 1543892) — this is an **index only** (no images; imageCount = 0). Consult it as a finding aid but recognize it is incomplete for the early decades.
- **Gap strategy:** Church records are the *de facto* vital records for this period.

### Church Records ⭐ Primary Source
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (collection ID 1612905) — the tool returned ~987,000 records. Covers the target period fully.
- **Key repository:** St. Louis Cathedral (Roman Catholic) registers from 1731, with gaps; held at the Archdiocese of New Orleans and microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Record types:** Baptisms (with parents, godparents, and frequently racial/social status noted), marriages, and burials
- **Language:** French and Spanish predominate pre-1812; English increasingly common after statehood
- **Multi-racial records:** Free persons of color (*gens de couleur libres*) appear in separate registers — researchers must check both the "white" and "free colored" registers for the same events
- **Access level:** **Indexed + images** via FamilySearch collection 1612905

### Census Records
- **Federal censuses available for this period:** 1810 (Orleans Territory), 1820, 1830, 1840 (Louisiana)
- **Note:** The 1800 federal census does not cover New Orleans (still under Spanish/French rule at enumeration)
- **Limitation:** Pre-1850 censuses list only the head of household by name; other household members appear only as tick marks by age/sex category
- **Substitute enumerations:** Spanish colonial censuses (*padrones*) survive for some years pre-1803 in the Cabildo records at the Louisiana State Archives

### Probate and Court Records (Successions)
- **Louisiana terminology:** Under civil law, "probate" is called **succession**. "Guardianship" is **tutorship**. "Incompetency" is **interdiction**.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* (collection ID 2078341) — ~456,000 records covering the target period
- **Where held:** Civil District Court of Orleans Parish (New Orleans); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)
- **Value:** Successions often name all heirs, describe property in detail, and list enslaved persons by name — exceptionally rich for family reconstruction
- **Access level:** **Indexed + images** via FamilySearch collection 2078341

### Notarial Records ⭐ Critical New Orleans Source
- **Repository:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — holds over 30 million pages from 1734 (per FamilySearch Wiki "New Orleans Genealogy")
- **Volume on FamilySearch:** One digitized volume found: *Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies), 1803–1820*, Orleans Parish — **167 images**, French and English, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**
  - **Access level: Browse-only images** — must be examined page by page; no search capability
- **Content:** Property transactions, contracts, wills, slave sales and manumissions, business partnerships, marriage contracts — the civil law equivalent of deed books, wills, and much more
- **Language warning:** Pre-1812 acts are predominantly in French or Spanish; a researcher must read the original language

### Land Records
- **System:** Louisiana uses a **civil law land system** with distinctive French/Spanish origins — arpents and toises (not acres and feet), long-lot surveys along waterways, and Spanish land grants (*mercedes*)
- **Key records:** Spanish land grants (pre-1803) are held at the General Land Office (BLM) and the Louisiana State Archives; American-era land patents (post-1803) are at the Bureau of Land Management GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov)
- **New Orleans specifically:** The city's lots were surveyed and recorded in notarial acts and the municipal cadastre
- Note: Louisiana is a **state-land state** (not a federal public land state), so the public land survey system applies only to areas beyond original Spanish/French grants

### Parish (Civil) Marriages
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957* (collection ID 1798054) — this collection begins **1837**, outside the early 1800s window
- **Gap:** No equivalent indexed civil marriage collection covers 1800–1837 on FamilySearch. Use **church marriage registers** (collection 1612905) for this gap period.

### Military Records
- **War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (1815):** Service records, pension files, and muster rolls for Louisiana militia and volunteers are at NARA and available on Fold3 (subscription)
- **Territorial militia:** Some militia muster rolls for Orleans Territory survive at the Louisiana State Archives
- **NARA access:** Fold3 (fold3.com, subscription) holds military records per the external links result

### Immigration Records
- **Port of New Orleans:** One of the busiest U.S. ports of entry. Passenger arrival lists begin in earnest after 1820.
- **NARA:** Passenger lists for New Orleans (1820 onward) are at NARA and available on Ancestry.com (subscription)
- **Pre-1820:** No systematic passenger manifests were required. Use notarial acts and church records for tracing new arrivals.
- **Note:** A large wave of Saint-Domingue (Haitian) refugees arrived 1809–1810 — check both church registers and notarial records for this cohort

### Newspaper Records
- **New Orleans had active newspapers** from the early 1800s: *Le Moniteur de la Louisiane* (French, from 1794), *Louisiana Gazette* (English, from 1804)
- **Where held:** Historic New Orleans Collection, Louisiana State University, and Newspapers.com (subscription, per external links result) hold runs of early Louisiana newspapers
- **Value:** Marriage notices, death notices, estate sale advertisements, sheriff's sales — particularly important given the weakness of civil vital registration

### Cemetery Records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823) — the oldest surviving above-ground tomb cemeteries in the U.S.
- **Sexton records:** Partially survive at the Archdiocese of New Orleans; some gaps due to yellow fever epidemic periods
- **FindAGrave:** findagrave.com (per external links result) has coverage for New Orleans cemeteries, though pre-1850 coverage is incomplete

### Tax Records
- **Territorial and state tax lists** for Orleans Parish survive at the Louisiana State Archives — useful as census substitutes, especially for years between federal enumerations
- **Spanish colonial tax records:** Some survive in Cabildo records pre-1803

### Records of Enslaved Persons and Free People of Color
- **Separate church registers** for free persons of color exist at St. Louis Cathedral — **must be searched separately** from white registers
- **Slave sacramental records:** Baptisms and marriages of enslaved persons were recorded by Catholic priests — these sometimes name owners, parents, and African origins
- **Notarial records:** Slave sales, manumissions, and freedom papers are extensively documented in the New Orleans Notarial Archives
- **Spanish-era freedom suits:** Coartación (self-purchase of freedom) cases are in Cabildo records

## Records NOT Online

The following record types are known to exist but are **not available in any online name-searchable database**:

- **Pre-1803 Spanish colonial records** (Cabildo administrative records) — physical at Louisiana State Archives and Louisiana State Museum
- **New Orleans Notarial Acts in full** — Only a 167-image browse-only microfilm volume (1803–1820) is on FamilySearch; the vast majority of the 30+ million-page Notarial Archives collection must be consulted in person in New Orleans
- **Orleans Parish civil court records** before their digitization window — in-person at Orleans Parish Civil District Court
- **Parish tax lists** — physical at Louisiana State Archives
- **Spanish colonial censuses** (*padrones*) — physical at Louisiana State Archives

## Substitute Sources When Primary Records Are Missing

| Missing Record | Best Substitutes |
|---|---|
| Civil birth certificates (none before 1914) | St. Louis Cathedral baptismal registers (collection 1612905); notarial birth declarations |
| Civil death certificates (sparse before 1914) | Church burial registers (collection 1612905); Louisiana Statewide Death Index from 1819 (collection 1543892, index only); newspaper death notices; cemetery sexton records |
| Civil marriage certificates (before 1837) | Church marriage registers (collection 1612905); notarial marriage contracts |
| Missing census years | Tax lists at Louisiana State Archives; Spanish colonial padrones; church membership/confirmation lists |
| Destroyed notarial acts | Spanish-era notarial copies (Spanish law required duplicate registers, improving survival); succession inventories in probate records (collection 2078341) |
| Records of enslaved ancestors | Separate Catholic sacramental registers for enslaved persons; notarial manumission and sale acts; succession inventories naming enslaved persons |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search church records before anything else.** For the early 1800s, Catholic sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral are the *de facto* vital records. FamilySearch collection 1612905 (*Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925*) is the first stop.

2. **Always check both racial registers.** St. Louis Cathedral maintained separate registers for white, free colored, and enslaved parishioners. Search all three — events for mixed-heritage families can appear across multiple registers.

3. **Expect French and Spanish.** Records before 1812 are predominantly in French or Spanish. Budget time for translation, or use a professional translator. FamilySearch's translation skill or a hired translator may be needed for notarial acts in particular.

4. **The notarial records are irreplaceable.** Under civil law, notarial acts document property, business, and family transactions with a depth unmatched in common-law states. A single notarial act can contain a will, a property inventory, the names of all heirs, and descriptions of enslaved persons. The in-person New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is a required stop for serious research.

5. **Louisiana uses "successions," not "probate."** Search under succession terminology when looking for estate records in FamilySearch (collection 2078341) and at the Louisiana State Archives.

6. **The Parish Marriages collection (1798054) starts in 1837** — do not rely on it for early 1800s marriage research. Use church registers instead.

7. **Federal census coverage begins with 1810** for New Orleans. The 1800 federal census does not include the city (it was not yet U.S. territory). The 1820, 1830, and 1840 censuses cover Orleans Parish.

8. **The fires of 1788 and 1794 predate your period** — records created after 1794 are intact at their holding repositories. The fires are most relevant when trying to trace families back through the late 18th century.

9. **Yellow fever gaps.** Epidemic years (especially 1817–1820 and the 1830s–1850s) created periods of disrupted record-keeping; register entries may be sparse or missing during peak epidemic seasons.

10. **The FamilySearch wiki pages for Louisiana and New Orleans did not return jurisdiction-specific content in this session** — consult the FamilySearch Research Wiki directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy and familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for the most current guidance.

---

> **Digitization summary:** The single most important online collection for this period is *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (FamilySearch, free, indexed + images). The notarial acts — arguably the richest source class — are almost entirely physical-access-only at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center. Expect significant in-person or correspondence research for any thorough investigation of New Orleans ancestors in the early 1800s.
