# Locality Guide: Chicago / Cook County, Illinois — Great Chicago Fire Era (c. 1850–1900)

## Jurisdiction Overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **County** | Cook County, Illinois |
| **Formed** | 1831 |
| **County seat** | Chicago |
| **Parent jurisdiction** | Illinois (state), United States |
| **Key event** | Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed ~300 people, left 100,000+ homeless |
| **Economy** | Railroad hub, meatpacking, grain trade, manufacturing, commerce |
| **Ethnic composition** | German, Irish, Scandinavian, Bohemian, Polish, English, and African American communities all present by 1871 |
| **Denominations** | Roman Catholic, Lutheran (German and Scandinavian), Methodist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Jewish synagogues |

---

## ⚠️ The Core Problem: Catastrophic Record Loss

The **Cook County Courthouse burned on October 8–9, 1871**, destroying the single repository that held the bulk of pre-fire official records. According to the Wikipedia article on the fire and the FamilySearch Wiki article *Cook County, Illinois Genealogy*, the following were destroyed or severely depleted:

- **Pre-fire civil birth and death registers**
- **Pre-fire deed books** (land ownership and transfers)
- **Pre-fire probate files** (wills, inventories, estate distributions)
- **Pre-fire court records** (naturalizations, civil suits, criminal cases)
- **Pre-fire tax rolls**
- **Many church registers** from parishes located in the fire zone

**This is the defining research challenge for Chicago before 1871.** Post-fire record sets largely begin in late 1871 or 1872.

---

## Known Record Losses vs. What Survived

| Record Type | Pre-Fire Fate | What Survives |
|---|---|---|
| Civil birth/death/marriage registers | **Destroyed** | Only post-fire records (from 1871); church records fill the gap |
| Deed books | **Destroyed** | Reconstructed deeds under the Burnt Record Act (1872) |
| Probate files | **Destroyed** | Partial reconstructed copies; FamilySearch has a browse-only volume |
| Court records (naturalizations etc.) | **Destroyed** | Partial reconstructed copies; post-fire series begins 1871+ |
| Tax rolls | **Destroyed** | No known substitute for most years |
| Church registers (fire zone parishes) | **Many destroyed** | Surviving parishes re-established registers; diocesan copies sometimes existed |
| Federal census (1850, 1860, 1870) | **SURVIVED** | Originals held in Washington, D.C. — not locally stored, so unaffected by fire |
| City directories (1840s onward) | **Survived** | Held at Newberry Library |
| Military records | **Survived** | Held at NARA, never locally stored |

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Start date:** Civil vital registration in Cook County effectively restarts with **1871**, the year of the fire. The birth, death, and marriage registers that pre-date the fire were destroyed.
- **FamilySearch collections (indexed + images):**
  - *Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940* — **1,450,000 records** (collection id: 2024189)
  - *Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947* — **980,000 records** (collection id: 1913456)
  - *Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920* — **620,000 records** (collection id: 1756321)
- **Gap:** For births, deaths, and marriages **before October 1871**, no Cook County civil register survives. Use church records as the primary substitute (see below).
- **Access:** Free at FamilySearch.org; indexed + images.

### Church Records ← Primary Pre-Fire Substitute

Church registers are the most important source for Chicago families **before 1871**, and they fill the civil registration gap for the post-fire period as well.

- **FamilySearch collection (indexed):** *Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925* — **285,000 records** (id: 1803978). Covers multiple denominations; spans both pre- and post-fire eras.
- **Archdiocese of Chicago** — The **Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds Catholic parish registers. Many parishes pre-date the fire; diocesan backup copies often survived even when local registers were destroyed.
- **Lutheran archives** — German and Scandinavian Lutheran congregations maintained registers, some of which survived. Contact the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA) Archives in Chicago.
- **Note:** Church records from parishes in the fire's path may be partially or fully destroyed; parishes on the north and south sides of the city often survived intact.
- **Language:** German Lutheran and Bohemian Catholic registers may be in German or Latin.

### Census Records ← Crucial Survivor

Federal census records for Chicago **survived the fire entirely** because the original schedules were held in Washington, D.C., not at the local courthouse.

| Census Year | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1850 | **Available** | Indexed + images, FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| 1860 | **Available** | Indexed + images |
| 1870 | **Available — especially critical** | The last pre-fire federal census; use this to establish where families lived before the disaster |
| 1880 | **Available** | Indexed + images |
| 1890 | **Largely destroyed** (national fire in 1921) | Only fragments survive nationally |
| 1900 | **Available** | Indexed + images |

- **Illinois state censuses:** Illinois conducted state enumerations in **1855 and 1865**, filling the gaps between federal censuses. Check state archives / FamilySearch for availability.
- **Mortality schedules, 1850–1885:** List persons who died in the year preceding each federal census. Valuable for identifying fire victims and pre-fire deaths.

### Land Records

- **Pre-fire deeds:** Destroyed in the courthouse fire.
- **Burnt Record Act (1872):** Illinois enacted this law requiring property owners to **re-file their deeds** with Cook County. These reconstructed records are the primary source for pre-fire land ownership. Held at the **Cook County Recorder of Deeds** and partially in the **Chicago Title and Trust Company** collection.
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company records:** Held at the **Chicago History Museum**. Insurance and title search records compiled from private sources after the fire are a vital substitute for the destroyed official deed books. The FamilySearch wiki specifically names this as a key resource.
- **Post-fire deed books:** Held at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds; some digitized on FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch volume (partially indexed):** *Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880* — imageGroupNumber 009982111, 112 images, **41% name-indexed**, not full-text searchable. Search directly where indexed; browse-only for the remaining 59%.

### Probate and Court Records

- **Pre-fire records:** Destroyed in the courthouse fire.
- **Reconstructed copies:** FamilySearch holds a digitized volume of *Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871* — imageGroupNumber 009982110, 38 images, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image-by-image. Consult if you need pre-fire probate or court evidence.
- **Post-fire records:** Cook County resumed recording wills, estate files, naturalizations, and court cases after 1871. Held at the **Cook County Circuit Court Archives** and the **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD)** at Northeastern Illinois University.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations** could be filed in any court of record (federal, state, or local); post-fire Cook County naturalizations are at IRAD.

### Military Records

Military records were never locally stored in Chicago and were unaffected by the fire.

- **Civil War service records and pension files:** NARA (Washington, D.C.); available on **Fold3** (subscription) and partially on FamilySearch.
- **Illinois Adjutant General records:** Illinois State Archives, Springfield.
- **Draft registrations (Civil War):** NARA; searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- The fire occurred just six years after the Civil War ended — many Chicago men were Civil War veterans with pension files that can document family relationships.

### Immigration and Naturalization Records

Chicago was a major immigrant destination; by 1870 it was one of the most ethnically diverse cities in the U.S.

- **Passenger arrival lists:** NARA; indexed on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and MyHeritage. For immigrants arriving via eastern ports (New York, Baltimore), search NARA Atlantic port records.
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-fire naturalizations were held in the courthouse and were destroyed. Post-fire naturalizations are at IRAD (Northeastern Illinois University). Some Germans and Irish naturalized in their port of entry before reaching Chicago.
- **Ethnic community records:** German, Irish, Bohemian, and Scandinavian mutual aid societies, fraternal organizations, and foreign-language churches maintained independent membership rolls and records that were often not in the courthouse.

### Newspapers ← Key Substitute Source

Newspapers are particularly valuable for the fire period — obituaries, fire victim lists, relief committee lists, and missing persons notices were published extensively.

- **Chicago Tribune** (founded 1847): Famously published even during the fire. Available on **Newspapers.com** and **ProQuest Historical Newspapers**. The Tribune published extensive lists of fire victims, displaced families, and relief recipients.
- **Chicago Times, Chicago Inter-Ocean**, and other papers also covered the disaster.
- **German-language press:** *Illinois Staats-Zeitung* serves the large German immigrant community.
- Physical collections at the **Newberry Library** and **Chicago History Museum**.

### Cemetery Records

Cemetery records are especially important for post-fire deaths, as civil death registration was still being re-established.

- **Graceland Cemetery** (est. 1860, north side) — survived the fire
- **Rosehill Cemetery** (est. 1859, north side) — survived the fire
- **Catholic, Jewish, and Lutheran cemeteries** throughout Cook County
- **FindAGrave.com:** Extensive coverage of Cook County cemeteries (linked via external resources for this place)
- Sexton records (burial registers) held by individual cemetery offices

### City Directories

City directories are one of the most important substitute sources for pre-fire Chicago because they were published by private companies and copies survive in libraries outside the fire zone.

- Annual Chicago directories from the **1840s onward** survived and are held at the **Newberry Library**.
- Directories give name, occupation, and address — useful for placing families in the city before and after the fire.
- Available in digitized form through the **Newberry Library Digital Collections** and partially on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Key Collections for Cook County | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1833–1925 (285K); Birth Certs 1871–1940 (1.45M); Death Records 1871–1947 (980K); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620K); reconstructed pre-fire court records (browse-only); post-fire property re-recordings (41% indexed) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | Federal census 1850–1940; Civil War service/pension; immigration passenger lists; city directories | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Civil War and other military records | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records, Cook County cemeteries | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Chicago Tribune and other Chicago papers | Subscription |
| **FamilySearch Wiki** | *Cook County, Illinois Genealogy* — guidance on fire-era substitutes and repositories | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** (Chicago) | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, genealogical collections | In-person; some digitized |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance/title records; personal papers; photographs; fire-related ephemera | In-person; some online |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD), Northeastern Illinois Univ.** | Cook County records post-1871: court, probate, naturalization | In-person; contact IRAD |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (pre- and post-fire) | In-person by appointment |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person / mail request |
| **Cook County Recorder of Deeds** | Burnt Record Act reconstructed deeds (post-1872); post-fire deed books | In-person / online portal |
| **Illinois State Archives** (Springfield) | Illinois state census 1855, 1865; Illinois Adjutant General records | In-person / online request |
| **NARA — Great Lakes Region** (Chicago) | Federal census originals; naturalization records; military records | In-person |
| **ELCA Archives** (Chicago) | German and Scandinavian Lutheran parish registers | In-person by appointment |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following record types are known to exist but have **no online digital equivalent**:

- **Burnt Record Act reconstructed deeds (1872+)** — physical volumes at Cook County Recorder of Deeds; the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum is the key companion source and is not digitized online
- **Full Catholic parish register series** — the Archdiocese archives hold registers that may extend beyond the FamilySearch church records collection; contact the Bernardin Archives directly
- **Cook County Circuit Court archives (post-fire)** — naturalizations, equity cases, guardianships; held at IRAD but not fully digitized
- **City directories pre-1871** (some years) — physical at Newberry Library; only select years have been digitized

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census.** This is the last pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families, and the originals survived in Washington. Establish where each family member was living and their neighbors before searching fire-era records.

2. **Assume civil vital records before 1871 are gone; go directly to church records.** The FamilySearch *Cook County, Chicago Church Records, 1833–1925* collection is your primary pre-fire substitute for births, marriages, and burials.

3. **The Burnt Record Act (1872) is the key to pre-fire land.** If your ancestor owned property before the fire, they had to re-file their deed after the fire under this law. Search the Cook County Recorder's records from 1872–1874 for reconstructed pre-fire deeds.

4. **Check newspapers for fire-period events.** The Chicago Tribune published lists of relief recipients, displaced persons, and fire victims. These are invaluable when no official vital record survives.

5. **Don't overlook the Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum.** Insurance and title research records compiled from private sources after the fire are a major substitute for the destroyed official deed books — named explicitly in the FamilySearch wiki.

6. **Illinois state censuses (1855, 1865) can place families before the fire.** The 1865 state census, six years before the fire, is particularly useful.

7. **Civil War pension files can document family structure.** Many Chicago men served in the Civil War (1861–1865). Their pension files (at NARA / Fold3) often include marriage certificates, children's names, and other vital facts that pre-date or post-date the fire.

8. **Ethnic community records often survived.** German mutual aid societies, Catholic schools, Bohemian fraternal organizations, and Jewish congregations maintained records independently of the courthouse. These private records were frequently stored outside the fire zone.

9. **The pre-fire reconstructed court records volume (imageGroupNumber 009982110) is browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, must be reviewed image by image. Allocate time accordingly if pre-fire probate or court evidence is needed.

10. **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki article *Cook County, Illinois Genealogy*** (URL: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy) for updated repository contacts and digitization progress. The wiki confirmed all key repositories and substitute source strategies used in this guide.

---

> **Summary for fire-era research:** The Great Chicago Fire of 1871 is the defining constraint of all Chicago genealogy before that date. The strategic sequence is: (1) lock in the family with the 1870 federal census; (2) search church records and city directories for pre-1871 vital events and addresses; (3) use the Burnt Record Act deeds and Chicago Title/Trust records for property; (4) pivot to the Cook County civil registers (1871+) for post-fire events; and (5) consult the Newberry Library, Chicago History Museum, and IRAD for records that have not been digitized.

## 📜 Locality Research Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (c. 1699–1762, with Spanish transition to 1800)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

The 1700s in Louisiana span **two colonial regimes** that directly affect where records were created and are now held:

| Period | Governing Power | Administration |
|---|---|---|
| c. 1699–1762 | **France** | Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur), based in New Orleans |
| 1762–1800 | **Spain** | Cabildo, Spanish governors |
| 1800–1803 | France (briefly) → U.S. (Louisiana Purchase 1803) | |

New Orleans was founded in **1718** and served as the colonial capital. The colony was organized into **military posts and districts** — not counties. Louisiana's familiar **parish system** (used instead of counties) descended from the Catholic ecclesiastical parishes established in this era. The **Code Noir** (Black Code) was the governing legal framework for the colony, requiring Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons and restricting religious practice to Catholicism — making the Catholic Church the de facto civil registrar for vital events.

> **Key research implication:** Records straddle two national archival systems (French and Spanish), and the transition in 1762 means some French-language record-keeping continued well into the Spanish period. Plan to search under **both** colonial regimes for families active in the mid-to-late 1700s.

---

### Record Types, Coverage & Access

#### 1. 🕍 Catholic Parish Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
**The single most important source for French colonial Louisiana family research.**

- The Code Noir required the Catholic Church to baptize all colonists and enslaved persons — **no other church was legally recognized**, so there are no Protestant registers from this era.
- **St. Louis Cathedral** in New Orleans holds registers from **1720** — among the oldest surviving registers in what is now the United States.
- Records are in **French** (pre-1762) and transition to **Spanish** afterward; researchers must read the original language or use translations.

**FamilySearch:** [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) (Collection 1612905)
- ~987,654 records / ~493,827 images — date range starts at 1718, fully within the French colonial window
- ⚠️ *Note:* Collection detail (indexing/browse level) could not be confirmed due to a permission restriction; verify at FamilySearch whether the 1700s portion is name-indexed or browse-only before searching.

**Physical repositories:**
- **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** — holds original parish registers
- Individual parish archives for registers not transferred to the Archdiocese

---

#### 2. ⚖️ Superior Council Records (Conseil Supérieur)
The governing body of French Louisiana produced the colony's **civil court and administrative record** — the closest equivalent to county court records. These include:

- **Land grants / concessions** — French Crown grants to settlers
- **Civil and criminal court proceedings**
- **Contracts** (sales, apprenticeships, partnerships)
- **Estate inventories** — extremely rich for family reconstructions
- **Slave sale and manumission records**

**Repository:** [Louisiana Historical Center](https://louisianastatemuseum.org/louisiana-historical-center), housed in the **Old U.S. Mint building**, New Orleans. Partially digitized. Records are in **French**.

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)"*

---

#### 3. 📝 Notarial Records
New Orleans hosts the **oldest continuous notarial office in North America**. Under French (and later Spanish) civil law, notaries recorded:

- Wills and testaments
- Marriage contracts / marriage settlements
- Property sales and transfers
- Business contracts

Records survive from **the 1730s onward** and are held at the:

**[New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center](https://notarialarchives.org/)** — open to the public. Records in **French** (1730s–1762) and **Spanish** (1762–onward), with French-language records continuing well past 1762.

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants"*

---

#### 4. 🪦 Probate Records
**FamilySearch:** [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) (Collection 2078341)
- ~456,789 records / ~228,394 images — the 1756 start date falls within the French colonial period
- ⚠️ Indexing level not confirmed (collection_read permission unavailable); check FamilySearch for whether 1700s volumes are name-indexed or browse-only.

Also held physically at the **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge).

---

#### 5. 🌾 Land Records / Concessions
French colonial land grants ("concessions") followed French civil law, not English common law. Key sources:

- **American State Papers: Public Lands** — documents French and Spanish land grant claims (widely available in print and online via HathiTrust and Google Books)
- **Louisiana State Land Office** (Baton Rouge) — holds survey records and confirmed grant documents
- **Superior Council records** (Louisiana Historical Center) — original grant proceedings

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants"*

---

#### 6. 📊 Colonial Censuses (Recensements)
The French colonial government conducted periodic census rolls of the colony. Several survive and are an excellent substitute for family records in the early 1700s, before many parishes were established.

**Repository:** [Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)](https://www.archives-nationales.culture.gouv.fr/fr/web/guest/anom), Aix-en-Provence, France
- Holds the official administrative correspondence, census rolls, and colonial registers for French Louisiana
- Some records have been microfilmed; a growing portion is digitized at the **ANOM online portal** (portail.culture.fr/anom)
- Records in **French**

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)"; Wikipedia, "French Louisiana"*

---

#### 7. 🪖 Military Records
French colonial military posts ("postes") maintained muster rolls and personnel records. Spanish-era military records are richer for the 1762–1800 window.

- **NARA** (National Archives) holds some records relating to the Louisiana territory
- **[Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/)** — military records, including some colonial-era material
- **ANOM** (Aix-en-Provence) — French colonial military correspondence and muster rolls

---

#### 8. 📰 Newspapers
The *Louisiana Gazette* and *Moniteur de la Louisiane* began publishing in the early 1800s, after the French colonial period — **no colonial-era newspapers survive for genealogical use** during the 1700s.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1718–1925; Probate Records 1756–1984 | Free online |
| **Louisiana Historical Center**, New Orleans | Superior Council records, colonial court/land records | In-person; partial digitization |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | Original parish registers | In-person / by request |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial records from 1730s | In-person; public access |
| **Louisiana State Archives**, Baton Rouge | Probate, land, state records | In-person |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France | Census rolls, administrative correspondence, colonial records | In-person + growing online portal |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal and territorial records | In-person + online |
| **Ancestry / Fold3** | Census, military records | Subscription |

---

### ⚠️ Critical Research Quirks

1. **Language barrier:** Pre-1762 records are in **French**; post-1762 records shift to **Spanish**, though French continued in use. Name spellings vary between French and Spanish renderings of the same individual — a "Jean-Baptiste Dupré" becomes "Juan Bautista Dupré."

2. **No civil registration:** There was no government-run vital registration. The **Catholic Church is the civil registrar** for this period — parish registers are your birth, marriage, and death certificates.

3. **Enslaved persons in the records:** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved people. Many enslaved individuals appear in **parish registers** and **Superior Council slave-sale records** — often named, sometimes with family relationships noted.

4. **"Parish" means two things:** In Louisiana, "parish" refers to both the Catholic ecclesiastical unit (the source of records) and the civil administrative unit that later replaced counties. These overlapped but were not identical.

5. **Search both colonial regimes:** Families active in the 1750s–1760s will have records under **both French and Spanish** administrations. Don't stop at 1762; the same family appears in both systems.

6. **ANOM is essential for the early 1700s:** Before 1720, there were almost no settled parishes — the colony was just beginning. The colonial census rolls and administrative records at ANOM in France are often the only documentary evidence for the earliest settlers (1699–c. 1720).

7. **FamilySearch indexing levels unconfirmed for colonial volumes:** Collection detail access was restricted during this survey. Verify at FamilySearch whether the 1700s portions of Church Records (1612905) and Probate Records (2078341) are name-searchable or must be browsed image-by-image.

---

### Suggested Starting Strategy

1. **Start at FamilySearch** with [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — broadest coverage of the French colonial period.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Coal Mining Region (Late 1800s, c. 1870–1910)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Core counties (anthracite region):** Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland — all in northeastern Pennsylvania. A second bituminous coal region operated in western Pennsylvania (Allegheny, Washington, Westmoreland, Fayette counties).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (state from 1787)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query — consult federal census manuscript schedules directly for county-level figures.
- **Economy:** Dominated by anthracite and bituminous coal extraction. Major operators included the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, the Lehigh Valley Coal Company, and Pennsylvania Railroad coal subsidiaries.
- **Ethnic composition (per Wikipedia):** Early waves of Irish and Welsh miners (1830s–1860s); later waves of Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian immigrants (1870s–1900s). German immigrants also present. Community structure was strongly ethnic — neighborhoods, churches, and mutual aid societies were often ethnicity-specific.
- **Religious denominations:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational (and Welsh Baptist), Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic, Slovak Greek Catholic, Italian Catholic, German Lutheran and Reformed, and various Protestant denominations. Ethnic parishes are the primary record keepers for many communities before statewide civil registration.
- **Key events:** Avondale Mine Disaster (1869, 110 killed; led to first mine safety law); Molly Maguires active in the 1870s; founding of United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) in 1890; frequent smaller mine disasters throughout the period.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Lackawanna County** was carved out of Luzerne County in **1878**. Researchers tracing families in the Scranton/Carbondale area must search **Luzerne County records for any event before 1878**, then shift to Lackawanna County records from 1878 onward. The colliery payroll ledger volume on FamilySearch (Lackawanna, image group 002240017) reflects this — it begins in 1878. For earlier Scranton-area events, search Luzerne County sources.
- All other major anthracite counties (Schuylkill, Carbon, Northumberland) had stable boundaries during the 1870–1910 period.
- Pennsylvania began **statewide civil registration of deaths in 1906** and marriages systematically in the 1880s. For vital events before those dates, church records are the primary alternative.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Births:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide birth registration during most of the late 1800s. The Death Certificates collection on FamilySearch begins in 1906 (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records, fully indexed with images), confirming that statewide civil registration was not in force for the core of the target period. For births in the 1870–1900 window, **church baptismal registers are the primary source**.
- **Marriages:** Two indexed collections on FamilySearch cover the period:
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* (collection 1921317): 524,189 records, 1,048,378 persons, 312,045 images — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* (collection 1571957): 312,045 records, 624,090 persons, 156,023 images — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* (collection 1502909): 198,765 records — **indexed, no images**
- **Deaths:** No statewide civil death registration exists for most of the 1870–1900 window. Church burial registers and cemetery records are the primary substitutes. The 1906 death certificates collection is useful for deaths occurring just after the target period and often includes birthplace and parents' names — valuable for immigrant families.

### Church Records

- **Critical for this region.** Ethnic parishes maintained separate registers by community. Irish and Welsh congregations date to the 1840s–1860s; Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Italian parishes were founded in the 1870s–1900s as immigrant waves arrived.
- FamilySearch holds *Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985* (collection 1401638): **1,245,830 records, 607,220 images — indexed + images.** This is the single most important FamilySearch collection for vital events in the coal region before civil registration.
- Church records typically record: baptisms (with parents' names, godparents, and often birthplace of parents), marriages (with witnesses), and burials.
- **Language note:** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Ukrainian parish registers may be in Latin or the heritage language. Welsh registers are generally in English or Welsh.
- Physical church archives: Contact individual parish offices or diocesan archives (Diocese of Scranton for Lackawanna/Luzerne; Diocese of Allentown for Schuylkill/Carbon; Diocese of Harrisburg for Northumberland).

### Census Records

- **Federal census:** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 census schedules fully cover the target period and are indexed and searchable. The **1890 census was almost entirely destroyed** by fire — use tax records, city directories, or church records to bridge that gap.
- Occupation is recorded in all of these schedules; miners appear as "miner," "coal miner," or specific occupations (e.g., "breaker boy," "mule driver," "fire boss").
- **Mortality schedules** (1870 and 1880) list deaths in the year preceding the census — particularly useful for documenting mine accident victims.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and available free on FamilySearch and by subscription on Ancestry.com.

### Occupational and Mining Records *(Distinctive to this region)*

This is the record class most unique to coal mining research. Three digitized volumes appear on FamilySearch for the target period:

| Volume | County | Date Range | Images | Digitization Level |
|--------|--------|------------|--------|--------------------|
| Mine Worker Employment Cards (002240015) | Schuylkill | 1870–1900 | 410 | **Indexed + images** (95% indexed, full-text searchable) |
| Mine Accident Reports (002240016) | Luzerne | 1870–1895 | 287 | **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text) |
| Colliery Payroll Ledgers (002240017) | Lackawanna | 1878–1900 | 199 | **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text) |

*Note: The volume_search returned 23 total results for Pennsylvania in this period — only the first page of 3 was retrieved above. Additional volumes may exist for other counties; a paginated search would surface them.*

- **State Mine Inspector Reports (from 1870):** Published annually by the Pennsylvania state government, these report fatal mine accidents with the victim's **name, age, nationality, and cause of death** — an invaluable source for identifying immigrant miners. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). Not currently digitized on FamilySearch per the wiki search result.
- **UMWA Records (from 1890):** The United Mine Workers of America's membership rolls and grievance files survive fragmentarily. Held at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and the Anthracite Heritage Museum in Scranton. Contact those institutions directly.
- Additional company records (payrolls, accident reports beyond what is digitized) survive at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** and local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties.

### Immigration and Naturalization Records

- **Critical for this community.** Most late-19th-century miners were foreign-born. Many entered through the **Port of Philadelphia** or **Port of New York**; passenger arrival lists are indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry.com. Examine the full manifest — all family members, including infants, are listed alongside the head of household.
- **Naturalization (pre-1906):** Before the federal naturalization law of 1906, declarations of intent and petitions could be filed in *any* court of record — federal, state, or county. Many miners naturalized in county courts of common pleas near the collieries.
  - *Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906)* are held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (per wiki_search result).
  - Check county courthouse records for Luzerne and Lackawanna as well.
- **Post-1906:** Federal courts handled naturalization; records are at NARA Philadelphia (Mid-Atlantic region).
- **Ancestry.com** holds curated U.S. naturalization collections (per external_links_search).

### Probate and Court Records

- *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* (collection 1999196): **893,214 records, 446,607 images — indexed + images** on FamilySearch.
- Court records (held at county courthouses and on FamilySearch/Ancestry) include naturalization petitions, guardianship records, and estate proceedings. Mining families often appear in accident liability cases.

### Military Records

- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Many of the older miners in the 1870s–1890s were Civil War veterans. Service records and pension files are at **NARA** (Washington, D.C.) and searchable on **Fold3** (per external_links_search) and Ancestry.com. Pennsylvania pension records may also be at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Spanish-American War (1898):** Some miners served; check NARA and Fold3.
- Veterans' census schedules (1890) are nearly entirely destroyed with the rest of the 1890 census.

### Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) is the leading online cemetery index for this region and is included in the FamilySearch-curated external links for Pennsylvania (per external_links_search).
- Mining town cemeteries include both denominational (Catholic, Protestant) and secular plots. Many ethnic communities maintained separate burial grounds.
- Physical sexton records: Contact local funeral homes and church offices.

### Newspaper Records

- **Newspapers.com** provides access to historical newspapers from the coal region and is among the FamilySearch-curated external links (per external_links_search).
- Local coal-region papers published obituaries, mine accident reports, naturalization notices, and legal notices — particularly valuable given the absence of statewide civil registration.
- Key papers to look for: *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, Schuylkill County, published from 1825); *Scranton Tribune*; *Wilkes-Barre Times-Leader*.

### Land Records

- Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** (metes and bounds system). Deeds are held at the county recorder of deeds office and may be on FamilySearch microfilm.
- Miners typically rented company housing rather than owning land — check colliery payroll and company store records rather than deed books for establishing residence.

### Tax Records

- County tax records can substitute for the destroyed 1890 census. Held at county courthouses; some are on FamilySearch microfilm (browse-only or unindexed).

### Mutual Aid and Fraternal Records

- Ethnic mutual aid societies (Polish National Alliance, Lithuanian Alliance of America, Slovak Catholic Sokol, Ancient Order of Hibernians for Irish miners) maintained membership rolls, death benefit records, and minutes. These are scattered — contact relevant ethnic historical societies.
- UMWA local lodge records (from 1890) survive fragmentarily at the Anthracite Heritage Museum.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for This Place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church & Town Records 1708–1985 (1.2M records); County Marriages 1885–1950 (524K); Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312K); Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (199K); Probate Records 1683–1994 (893K); Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M); Mine Worker Employment Cards Schuylkill 1870–1900 (indexed); Mine Accident Reports Luzerne 1870–1895 (browse-only); Colliery Payroll Ledgers Lackawanna 1878–1900 (browse-only) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1870, 1880, 1900); passenger lists; naturalization records | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records statewide | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers including coal-region titles | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| **NARA online (archives.gov)** | Federal records including post-1906 naturalization | Free/fee |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector reports from 1870; Schuylkill County naturalization records 1840s–1906; state government records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| **County Courthouses** (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland) | Deeds, probate, naturalization petitions, court records | In-person / mail request |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Local mining company records, UMWA materials, local histories | In-person |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton / Lackawanna) | Mining community records, UMWA local records, ethnic society materials | In-person |
| **Diocesan Archives** (Scranton, Allentown, Harrisburg) | Church registers not yet microfilmed or digitized | Contact by mail/email |
| **Family History Library / FamilySearch Centers** | Microfilm of county records, church registers | In-person or loan to local center |

---

## Records NOT Online

- **State Mine Inspector annual reports (1870 onward):** Fatal accident lists with names, ages, nationalities — at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Not digitized on FamilySearch.
- **Most UMWA local lodge records:** Fragmentarily held at the Anthracite Heritage Museum.
- **Ethnic mutual aid society records:** Polish National Alliance, Lithuanian Alliance, Ancient Order of Hibernians, Slovak organizations — scattered, not systematically digitized.
- **Company store records and boarding house ledgers:** Survive only partially at county historical societies.
- **Many pre-1906 county naturalization records** outside Schuylkill County: Check individual county courthouses or the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Most colliery payroll records beyond the three FamilySearch volumes:** Physical holdings at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies.

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1890 U.S. Federal Census:** Virtually entirely destroyed by fire in 1921. Use 1889–1891 tax records, city directories, church membership rolls, and UMWA records to reconstruct this gap.
- No major courthouse fires are documented for the primary anthracite counties in the target period, but always verify current courthouse holdings before assuming records survive.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with church records before civil registration.** Pennsylvania had no statewide birth registration before the early 1900s. For births and early deaths, the FamilySearch *Church and Town Records* collection (1.2 million records) is your first stop — but identify which ethnic congregation the family would have attended.

2. **Identify the ethnic parish.** A Welsh miner in Pottsville attended a different church than an Irish or Polish miner three streets away. Knowing nationality narrows the search to the right register. Nationality is often listed in the census occupation column or in Mine Inspector accident reports.

3. **Use Mine Inspector Reports to anchor immigrant families.** The annual reports (1870 onward, Pennsylvania State Archives) name accident victims with age, nationality, and sometimes township. A fatality record can confirm a person's presence, employer, and national origin even when no other record is found.

4. **For the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878, search Luzerne County.** Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878 — all earlier records for that area are filed under Luzerne County at the courthouse and in FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

5. **The 1890 census gap is significant.** Bridge it with: county tax lists (courthouse), city directories (local libraries and online via Ancestry), church membership rolls, and UMWA records if the miner was a member after 1890.

6. **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill, FamilySearch image group 002240015)** are 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable — the most accessible mining-specific record online. Search these early if your ancestor was in Schuylkill County.

7. **Luzerne Mine Accident Reports (image group 002240016) and Lackawanna Colliery Payroll Ledgers (002240017)** are browse-only with no name index. You will need to know the approximate colliery or year range before browsing image by image.

8. **Naturalization records reveal the home village.** Post-1906 federal petitions often include the specific town of birth in the old country — essential for tracing immigrant origins. Pre-1906 county court declarations are shorter but still establish arrival date and country of origin.

9. **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki page on Pennsylvania Occupational Records** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records) for additional guidance on company and mining records.

10. **Consider DNA testing** alongside documentary research for immigrant lines where village-of-origin records have not been located — particularly useful for connecting to relatives who remained in Ireland, Wales, Poland, or Slovakia.

---

The bituminous coal region of western Pennsylvania uses many of the same record types but different county repositories — let me know if you need a separate guide for that area.*

## 📜 Locality Research Guide: Massachusetts Early Puritan Settlements (1620–1700)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

The early 1600s in Massachusetts involved **two separate colonies** that must be researched independently:

- **Plymouth Colony** (1620–1691) — founded by the Pilgrims/Separatists; governed independently and kept its own court, land, and vital records. Its records are published and indexed as a distinct body.
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (1628–1691) — the larger Puritan colony; absorbed Plymouth Colony by royal charter in 1691, at which point the combined entity became the **Province of Massachusetts Bay**.

Massachusetts was among the earliest jurisdictions in North America to mandate civil vital registration: **the General Court required towns to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in 1639.** Four counties were established in 1643 (Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and Suffolk), creating county-level courts, land registries, and probate jurisdiction. Researchers must work at both the **town level** (for vital records) and the **county level** (for deeds, probate, and court records).

> ⚠️ **Key quirk:** Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are organized and published *separately* from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Always check both bodies, especially for pre-1691 research. After 1691, both fall under Massachusetts Bay Province.

> ⚠️ **Key quirk:** The original Norfolk County (est. 1643) included towns now in New Hampshire. If your ancestor was in that region, records may be filed under colonial Norfolk County, not any modern county.

---

### Population Context

Population data for colonial Massachusetts was not available through the FamilySearch tools. Historically, the Great Migration (1630–1640) brought approximately **20,000 settlers** to Massachusetts Bay Colony (per the Wikipedia article on Massachusetts Bay Colony). By 1700, the combined colonial population was roughly 55,000–70,000.

---

### Record Types, Coverage & Access

#### 1. 📋 Town Vital Records — **Primary source for births, marriages & deaths**
- **What:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by town clerks per the 1639 mandate.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (Collection ID: 2061550) — 3,456,789 records spanning the full colonial period. Direct URL: [familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)
- **Published compilation:** The **Tanner-Corbin "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns — a critical finding aid. Many volumes are digitized on Google Books and Internet Archive.
- **Access note:** Per-volume indexing detail (% name-indexed) could not be retrieved in this session; treat early 1600s entries as potentially browse-only and cross-check against the published Tanner-Corbin abstracts.
- **Gaps:** Early compliance was imperfect — not all town clerks recorded events promptly in the 1630s–1640s. If a vital record is missing, turn to church records.

#### 2. ⛪ Church Records (Congregational) — **Critical substitute and supplement**
- **What:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). Congregational was the *established church* of the colony — these records often predate and supplement town records.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (Collection ID: 1921657) — 987,654 records. URL: [familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)
- **Published:** Many early church records appear in the **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** publications series and in local historical society volumes. NEHGS holds substantial manuscript church record collections.
- **Access note:** Indexing level for early volumes not confirmed; plan to browse images for pre-1650 entries.
- **Gaps:** Not all early Congregational churches kept continuous registers. Some records were held in ministers' personal papers, so check biographical records of the minister as well.

#### 3. 📜 Probate Records — **Estate, guardianship & inventory records**
- **What:** Wills, inventories, administration bonds, guardianship appointments. Probate jurisdiction was at the county level from the 1630s.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* (Collection ID: 1678901) — 567,890 records. URL: [familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)
- **Physical records:** Original volumes held at **county probate courts**; the Massachusetts Archives also holds early colonial probate material.
- **Note:** Plymouth Colony probate is published separately — consult *Plymouth Colony: Its History and People, 1620–1691* and the published *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth*.

#### 4. 🏡 Land Records (Deeds & Town Proprietors' Records)
- **What:** Deeds, land grants, and town proprietors' records. County deed registries opened in the 1630s. Town proprietors' books (recording original land division) are equally important for this period.
- **FamilySearch coverage:** No separate land/deed collection appeared in the FamilySearch collections search for the 1600–1700 window — this is a digitization gap on FamilySearch for early colonial deeds.
- **Physical records:** Held at **county registries of deeds** (Registry of Deeds offices for Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, and Plymouth counties all have early colonial volumes). The **Massachusetts Archives** holds some original land records.
- **Published:** Early deeds and town grant records appear in many published town histories.

#### 5. ⚖️ Court Records — **Colony-level judicial and administrative records**
- **What:** General Court records, county court records (civil, criminal, equity), and Quarter Sessions. Court files frequently name family relationships, land transactions, and community disputes.
- **Repository:** The **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) holds the original Massachusetts Bay Colony records, General Court records, Governor's correspondence, and court records from the 1620s onward.
- **Published:** The multi-volume *Records of the Governor and Company of the Massachusetts Bay in New England* (Shurtleff edition) is published and widely available.
- **Plymouth Colony courts:** Published in *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth in New England* (Shurtleff & Pulsifer edition, 12 vols.).
- **FamilySearch coverage:** No indexed court records collection for the 1600–1700 window appeared in the search results.

#### 6. 🚢 Immigration & Passenger Lists — **Arrivals 1620–1650**
- **FamilySearch gap:** The FamilySearch *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists* collection (ID: 1784312) covers **1820–1891 only** — it does not include colonial-era arrivals. This is a significant gap for 1600s research.
- **Primary published resource:** The **Great Migration Study Project** (New England Historic Genealogical Society / Robert Charles Anderson) documents every known immigrant to New England 1620–1643 with full biographical sketches. Volumes cover alphabetically organized immigrants, citing all known primary sources. Available in print and through NEHGS digital library (americanancestors.org).
- **Other sources:** John Camden Hotten's *Original Lists of Persons of Quality…Emigrants…Who Went from Great Britain to the American Plantations* (1874); Charles Banks's *The Planters of the Commonwealth* (1930).

#### 7. 🗺️ Colony & Provincial Records
- **What:** Governor's council minutes, legislative acts, land grants, oaths of allegiance, lists of freemen (voters admitted to the colony).
- **Repository:** **Massachusetts Archives**, 220 Morrissey Blvd., Boston, MA 02125. Holds the original colony records.
- **Online:** Some are available through the Massachusetts Archives digital collections portal (mass.gov/orgs/massachusetts-archives).
- **Published:** *Records of the Governor and Company of Massachusetts Bay* (Shurtleff); *Plymouth Colony Records* (Shurtleff & Pulsifer).

#### 8. 📰 Newspapers (Very Limited)
- No Massachusetts newspaper was published before 1690 (the *Publick Occurrences* appeared briefly in 1690; the *Boston News-Letter* began in 1704). Newspapers are not a viable source for most of the 1600s.

#### 9. ❌ Records That Do NOT Apply to This Period
| Record Type | Why Not Applicable |
|---|---|
| Federal Census | Begins 1790 |
| Massachusetts Passenger Lists (FS) | Begins 1820 |
| Massachusetts Naturalization Records (FS) | Begins 1790 |
| State Vital Registration | Massachusetts began statewide registration in 1841 |
| Civil War / Military Pension Records | Post-period |

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Colony records, General Court, governor's papers, court records from 1620s | In-person; some digitized at mass.gov |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Largest genealogical library in New England; manuscript collections, Great Migration series, published genealogies | americanancestors.org (subscription); in-person at 99 Newbury St., Boston |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Town vital records (1620–), church records (1630–), probate (1635–) | Free online |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Land deeds from 1630s (Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, Plymouth counties) | In-person; some county registries have online portals |
| **County Probate Courts** | Probate files from 1630s | In-person; partial digitization on FamilySearch |
| **American Antiquarian Society** (Worcester, MA) | Colonial printed materials, newspapers, town histories | In-person by appointment; some digital |
| **Pilgrim Hall Museum** (Plymouth, MA) | Plymouth Colony material, Mayflower passenger resources | pilgrimhall.org |

---

### Recommended Research Strategy

1. **Start with the Great Migration Study** (NEHGS) if your ancestor arrived before 1643 — it is the most thoroughly sourced finding aid for this cohort.
2. **Search the FamilySearch Town Vital Records collection** (2061550) and cross-check against the Tanner-Corbin published abstracts.
3. **Search Congregational church records** (FS collection 1921657) especially for events missing from town records.
4. **Determine the county** your ancestor's town fell under in the 1640s–1690s — then search that county's probate and deed records.
5. **Remember the two-colony distinction**: confirm whether your ancestor was in Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) or Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691) — the records bodies are separate until the 1691 merger.
6. **Consult NEHGS / americanancestors.org** for manuscript collections, emigrant origins research, and published colonial genealogies not available elsewhere.

---

| Colonial passenger lists | ❌ FS collection begins 1820 | Great Migration Study (NEHGS) |
| Census | ❌ Federal census begins 1790 | n/a |

Treat pre-1650 entries in all three as potentially browse-only images, and always cross-reference the published Tanner-Corbin abstracts and the Great Migration Study.

# 🗺️ Oklahoma Territory — Land Run Era (c. 1880–1910) Locality Guide

## Jurisdictional Context

The Land Run of 1889 settled what had been called the **Unassigned Lands** — territory with no organized civil government for settlers. Three milestones shape which records exist and where they live:

| Date | Event | Record Impact |
|---|---|---|
| **April 22, 1889** | Land Run opens; ~50,000 claimants; land offices open in Guthrie and Kingfisher | Federal homestead files begin immediately |
| **May 2, 1890** | Organic Act creates **Oklahoma Territory** (western half); Indian Territory (eastern half, Five Civilized Tribes) remains separate | Territorial courts, tax rolls, and county records begin |
| **November 16, 1907** | The two territories merge into the **State of Oklahoma** | County vital registration begins 1908 |

> **Critical split:** Oklahoma Territory (western counties, Land Run area) and Indian Territory (eastern counties, tribal nations) were administered separately until 1907. If you don't yet know which half your ancestor settled in, you must work both administrative trails — they do not share record systems.

---

## Record Classes and Access

### 1. ⭐ Homestead & Land Records — **Indexed + Images (FamilySearch)**

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* — 234,567 records, 117,283 images
([familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872))

- Each homestead file at NARA Washington, D.C. **(Record Group 49, General Land Office)** contains the original application, witnesses' testimony, proof of five-year settlement, and the final patent. **Rejected applications also survive** and often hold more family detail than approved ones.
- **BLM General Land Office Records** (glorecords.blm.gov): Partially indexed online — free to search and download patent images.
- Files typically name the claimant's state of origin, making them an anchor for tracing the pre-Oklahoma migration trail.
- Source per FamilySearch Wiki article *"Oklahoma Land Records — Land Run and Homestead Records"*

### 2. ⭐ Indian Censuses and Rolls — **Indexed + Images (FamilySearch)**

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* — 567,890 records, 283,945 images
([familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432))

- The **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** are the definitive enrollment of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole, Chickasaw). Any ancestor with Indian Territory ancestry must be checked here.
- Also useful for non-Native researchers whose ancestors interacted with tribal land systems or appear as witnesses/neighbors in tribal records.

### 3. County Marriages — **Indexed + Images (FamilySearch)**

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* — 456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images
([familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789))

- Coverage begins in 1890 with the formation of Oklahoma Territory counties. Originals at county courthouses and the Oklahoma Historical Society.

### 4. Mission and Church Records — **Indexed + Images (FamilySearch)**

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* — 123,456 records, 61,728 images
([familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321))

- Congregations formed sporadically starting in 1889 as denominations moved into the new towns. For 1889–1907, church registers are often the **only** documentation of births and deaths (see vital records gap below).

### 5. Census Records

| Census | Coverage | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **1880 Federal Census** | Entire U.S. — search your family *before* the Land Run, in their origin state (Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas) | FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** ⭐ | One of the very few surviving 1890-era census records in the nation — documents settlers just one year after the Land Run | **Oklahoma Historical Society**; FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| **1900 Federal Census** | Oklahoma Territory (territorial) | FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| **1910 Federal Census** | Oklahoma (state) | FamilySearch, Ancestry |

> **Gap alert:** The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed in a 1921 fire. Oklahoma's 1890 territorial special census is the primary substitute — do not skip it.

### 6. Territorial Court Records (1890–1907)

- **National Archives at Fort Worth** and **Oklahoma State Archives** hold district court civil/criminal cases, probate, and naturalization records for Oklahoma Territory (source: FamilySearch Wiki, *"Oklahoma Territorial Records — Territorial Courts and Early Settlement"*).
- Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any territorial court of record.
- Probate files name heirs, establishing kinship; guardianship records name minors.
- **Sooner contest files**: Disputed land claims were litigated — contested-claim court files (NARA Fort Worth) are genealogically rich for families whose entry was challenged.
- **Digitization status:** Not comprehensively digitized — physical or microfilm access is typically required.

### 7. Vital Records (Birth & Death)

> ⚠️ **Oklahoma did not require statewide vital registration until 1908** — one year after statehood. For the period 1889–1907 there are **no civil birth or death records**. Substitute sources:
- Church baptism and burial registers (see Mission & Church Records above)
- Death notices and obituaries in territorial newspapers
- Cemetery transcriptions (Find A Grave; county historical societies)
- Family Bible records (often held by county historical societies or in private hands)

Post-1908 records are at the **Oklahoma State Department of Health**, with access restrictions on recent decades.

### 8. Military Records

- **Fold3** (fold3.com) and **NARA**: Service records and pension files, including Oklahoma volunteers in the Spanish-American War (1898).
- **WWI Draft Registrations (1917–1918)**: Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry — useful for locating men who had settled in Oklahoma by then and for capturing birthplace and physical descriptions.

### 9. Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com): Indexed statewide. Many early Land Run settlers were buried in rural family plots; county historical societies often hold supplementary transcriptions not yet online.

### 10. Historical Newspapers

- **Newspapers.com**: Territorial-era Oklahoma newspapers. Guthrie and Oklahoma City papers (*The Oklahoma State Capital*, *Oklahoma Daily Times-Journal*) launched immediately in 1889 — land claim contest notices, legal filings, and settler lists were routinely published.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | 4 digitized Oklahoma collections (all indexed + images); 1890 territorial census | Free online |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents and homestead certificates | Free online |
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Territorial court records (RG 21), Indian Territory records | In-person / NARA request |
| **NARA Washington, D.C.** (RG 49) | General Land Office homestead application files | In-person / NARA request |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (okhistory.org) | 1890 territorial census, territorial newspapers, county histories | Online catalog; some digital |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** (das.ok.gov) | Territorial court records, post-1908 vital records | In-person; some online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses (1880–1910), Dawes Rolls, passenger lists | Subscription |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Military service records, pension files | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions statewide | Free online |
| **Newspapers.com** | Territorial-era Oklahoma newspapers | Subscription |

## Research Strategy & Gotchas

1. **Start in the origin state.** The 1889 Land Run drew settlers primarily from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Arkansas. Search the 1880 federal census there to establish the family *before* Oklahoma — homestead files will then confirm where they went.

2. **Know which territory.** Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east) had completely separate civil administrations until 1907. Records do not cross over. Determine your county first, then identify which jurisdiction it fell under.

3. **Rejected homestead applications are research gold.** NARA's RG 49 files include rejected claims, which often contain more witness testimony and family detail than the approved patents.

4. **County formation was rapid and chaotic.** Oklahoma Territory counties were organized from 1890 onward; boundaries shifted frequently. Always verify a county's formation date before assuming a courthouse holds records from a given year — earlier records may be in a parent county or at the territorial level.

5. **No civil vital records before 1908.** Plan entirely around substitutes (church, newspapers, cemetery) for the 1889–1907 window.

6. **Dawes Rolls are the gateway to Five Civilized Tribes ancestry.** Any ancestor enrolled in Indian Territory (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole, or Chickasaw) appears in the Dawes Rolls — the single most important record for eastern-Oklahoma lineages.

7. **The FamilySearch Oklahoma wiki page** did not resolve to Oklahoma-specific content in this survey. Consult the wiki directly at **familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy** for the most current collection guidance.

---

## Coverage Gaps Noted

- **No population data** was returned for Oklahoma in the FamilySearch place-population tool.
- **Territorial court records** at NARA Fort Worth are not comprehensively digitized — physical or microfilm research is typically required.
- **Church records before 1900** are spotty; many early congregational registers from 1889–1895 do not survive.
- **FamilySearch wiki place pages** for Oklahoma returned only generic content — Oklahoma-specific wiki articles should be consulted directly.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (c. 1780–1819, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** The region now called Alabama was organized as part of the **Mississippi Territory** on April 7, 1798, carved from land ceded by Georgia and Spain. The eastern portion became the **Alabama Territory** on March 3, 1817, and Alabama achieved statehood on December 14, 1819.
- **Administrative centers:** Natchez (Mississippi Territory capital); St. Stephens, then Cahaba (Alabama Territory capital)
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–)
- **Special exception — Mobile area:** The Mobile District remained under **Spanish control until April 15, 1813**, so residents of that area before 1813 appear in Spanish colonial records, not American territorial records.
- **Population:** No FamilySearch population data was returned for this period. Wikipedia confirms the region was sparsely settled early in this period; migration accelerated sharply after the Creek War of 1813–1814, with settlers arriving from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, frontier trading; cotton cultivation expanding rapidly after 1813.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations throughout; Anglo-American settlers (mostly from the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia); French Creole and Spanish Creole communities in the Mobile area; enslaved African Americans increasing rapidly.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile area, Spanish period); Methodist and Baptist circuit riders serving frontier Anglo settlers; no established churches in most of the territory until the 1810s.
- **Key events:** Creek War of 1813–1814 (Battle of Horseshoe Bend); U.S. seizure of Mobile from Spain (1813); massive land rush following the Creek cessions.

---

## Boundary Changes — Critical for Researchers

This is the defining challenge of this period. **Records follow the creating jurisdiction, not modern Alabama boundaries.** You must work three overlapping research trails simultaneously:

1. **1780–1798 (colonial):** The Mobile area was under Spanish administration. The rest of what is now Alabama had no formal American civil record-keeping infrastructure.
2. **1798–1817 (Mississippi Territory):** All of present-day Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory. Records created in this period are filed under that territory. The FamilySearch collections for **Mississippi** (not Alabama) are therefore the starting point for this period's courthouse-type records.
3. **1817–1819 (Alabama Territory):** The eastern part of the Mississippi Territory was reorganized as Alabama Territory. Records from this brief period begin to appear in Alabama-scope collections.
4. **County formation:** Individual county records begin only when each county was officially organized. Washington County (SW Alabama area) and Madison County (north Alabama) were the earliest; Baldwin County organized 1809. **Always identify which county existed for a specific location and date before searching.**

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** Alabama did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1908**. There is no civil birth/death registration for the territorial period.
- **Marriages:** County-level marriage bonds and registers begin at county formation — the earliest Alabama county marriages on FamilySearch begin **1809** (collection 1598408: *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950*; 612,345 records, 1,224,690 persons, 306,172 images — **indexed + images**).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see below) and probate records are the only sources for vital events before county formation.

### Church Records
- **Catholic (Mobile area):** The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Mobile has sacramental registers going back to the Spanish period. FamilySearch's *Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950* (collection 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images — **indexed + images**) begins 1803 and includes some Catholic registers. Original Spanish-period church records are held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville; the Library of Congress holds copies. The Mobile Municipal Archives holds microfilm of French colonial church records.
- **Protestant (frontier settlers):** Methodist and Baptist circuit records are scattered and often lost. Some appear in the FamilySearch Alabama Church Records collection. Denomination archives (United Methodist Church Commission on Archives and History; Southern Baptist Historical Library and Archives) hold additional material not confirmed digitized for this period.
- **Language note:** Catholic registers from the Mobile area in this period may be in **French or Spanish** — researchers must be able to read the original.
- **Mississippi-scope church records:** FamilySearch collection 2034891 (*Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950*; 87,654 records, 43,827 images — **indexed + images**) covers the territorial period and may include records for the Alabama portion of the territory.

### Census Records
- **Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808):** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, and 1808 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (*Alabama Genealogy*, "Territorial Records" section), these are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery. FamilySearch's volume search returned **no digitized browsable volumes** for this period — these are **physical/microfilm** holdings at ADAH, not confirmed online.
- **Federal census 1810:** The first federal census to enumerate most Alabama-area settlers. Covered by FamilySearch collection 2016756 (*Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890*; 287,634 records — **index only, no images on FamilySearch**). The 1810 census images are available on Ancestry.com. **Note:** The Mobile District under Spanish control in 1810 is NOT in the U.S. federal census.
- **Mississippi-scope census substitutes:** FamilySearch collection 1927171 (*Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890*; 198,340 records — **index only, no images**) covers 1792 onward and includes territorial-era substitutes for what is now Alabama.
- **No state census** was conducted during the territorial period.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Alabama scope:** FamilySearch collection 1537764 (*Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985*; 438,210 records, 219,105 images — **indexed + images**) begins at county formation (1809 earliest). This is one of the richest sources for reconstructing families in this period.
- **Mississippi Territory scope:** FamilySearch collection 1855293 (*Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920*; 245,670 records, 122,835 images — **indexed + images**) covers the territorial period and will include court actions filed for what is now Alabama.
- Territorial court records are also held physically at ADAH and at the Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH) in Jackson.

### Land Records ⭐ *Most Important Source for this Period*
- **Federal land patents:** Alabama is a **public-domain (federal land) state** — the U.S. government disposed of land through the General Land Office. Land entries and patents from the territorial period are searchable at the **BLM General Land Office Records** website (glorecords.blm.gov), free and online, with images of original patents.
- **FamilySearch — Mississippi Territory land records:** Collection 1919694 (*Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907*; 312,450 records, 156,225 images — **indexed + images**). This collection begins at the very start of the territorial period (1798) and is the primary FamilySearch source for land transactions during the years when present-day Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory. **Search this under Mississippi-scope, not Alabama-scope.**
- **Spanish and British colonial grants (Mobile area):** Pre-American land grants are held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) with copies at the Library of Congress. The BLM GLO Records also include confirmed Spanish/British grants that were validated by the U.S. government.
- **Tax records as land substitutes:** Territorial tax lists are among the records held at ADAH (physical/microfilm; not confirmed digitized).

### Military Records
- **Creek War (1813–1814):** Service and pension records for participants are at NARA. Fold3 holds digitized military records for this period.
- **War of 1812:** Alabama-area settlers serving in the militia appear in War of 1812 records at NARA. Pension application files often contain detailed family information.
- **Territorial militia rolls:** Mentioned in the FamilySearch Wiki as a territorial record type held at ADAH — not confirmed digitized.
- **Access:** Fold3 (subscription) and NARA (in-person or by mail/digitization request, or through Ancestry) are the primary online points of access.

### Cemetery Records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave indexes many Alabama cemeteries, including early ones, though coverage for pre-1820 burials is sparse for the interior. FindAGrave is not a confirmed curated FamilySearch external link for Alabama specifically, but the generic link was returned.
- **Physical records:** Church burial grounds and family cemeteries predominate for this period; formal sexton records are rare this early.

### Newspaper Records
- **Coverage is thin.** Newspapers.com was returned as a generic resource. Territorial-era newspapers were few; *The Mobile Centinel* (est. 1811) and *Halcyon and Tombeckbee Public Advertiser* are among the earliest. Digitized coverage on Newspapers.com for pre-1820 Alabama is sparse. Check the Library of Congress Chronicling America database (free, chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) for any digitized territorial newspapers.

### Immigration / Emigration
- **Relevant context:** Most settlers in this period were internal migrants from the southeastern states, not recent European immigrants. Immigration records (passenger lists) are not a primary source type for most Alabama territorial-period families.
- **Spanish Colonial period:** Incoming settlers to the Mobile District during the Spanish period may appear in Spanish provincial records (Archivo General de Indias).

---
